title: Disrupting a Criminal Scam Operation
summary: OpenAI disrupted a Cambodia-based scam operation using ChatGPT to support investment, romance, gambling, and impersonation schemes.
full_text:
Disrupting a Criminal Scam Operation
OpenAI disrupted a Cambodia-based scam operation using ChatGPT to support investment, romance, gambling, and impersonation schemes.
Introduction
Earlier this year, we disrupted a Cambodia-based scam operation that used ChatGPT to support investment, romance, gambling, and law enforcement impersonation schemes. We began investigating this activity following a lead from our peers at WhatsApp and have since shared additional threat signals with industry partners and relevant authorities.
The operation illustrates an important reality about modern scam networks: organized criminal groups rarely restrict themselves to a single type of scam. Instead, they opportunistically employ whatever narratives, personas, and tactics they think will be most effective to deceive victims. In our investigations we routinely observe actors moving between scam types, or combining multiple scam techniques within a single operation.
Some users in the network also generated content suggesting links to human trafficking and forced criminality. These observations are consistent with extensive public reporting(opens in a new window) describing(opens in a new window) organized crime groups in Southeast Asia that recruit workers with promises of legitimate employment before trapping them in systems of debt bondage and coercion. While we cannot independently determine the circumstances of every individual involved, the activity serves as a reminder that the people conducting scams can themselves be victims of exploitation.
Actor
We banned a coordinated network of ChatGPT accounts that very likely originated in Cambodia, and was likely operating in or around Poipet, a city in Banteay Meanchey province that public reporting(opens in a new window) has repeatedly(opens in a new window) linked(opens in a new window) to online scam compounds and trafficking operations.
The network used our models to create and support the operation of fake online personas, generate and translate messages sent to scam targets, create promotional content for their fraudulent schemes, and assist with day-to-day operations.
As with past(opens in a new window) scam networks we have disrupted, a subset of users also employed ChatGPT for administrative work, including drafting internal announcements, translating messages between staff, and documenting matters that appeared related to recruitment, immigration status, working conditions, and employee discipline.
Behavior
The network simultaneously conducted multiple types of scams, often blending elements from different schemes. For instance, operators used dating personas to build trust before introducing fraudulent investment opportunities involving cryptocurrencies and spot gold trading. Other users engaged in lengthy romantic conversations with targets using fictitious identities, posed as representatives of online gambling platforms offering fake bonuses and winnings, or impersonated law enforcement agencies to tell targets they needed to pay fines for committing serious criminal offenses.
Although the narratives varied, users across the network consistently displayed the same underlying pattern of deceptive behavior. For example, they created and operated fake dating profiles, fictitious investment experts, and fraudulent law enforcement personas. They also generated images of forged documents, including passports, legal notices, stock-purchase confirmations, and gambling platform interfaces.
As we’ve highlighted in(opens in a new window) previous(opens in a new window) reports(opens in a new window), the scammers followed a common pattern in their interactions with targets, which we think of as the ping (outreach), the zing (generate emotion), and the sting (extract money).
- The ping: The network used ChatGPT to translate and generate conversations with targets on messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram. Scammers also created social media content and researched dating profile material to support their fake personas.
- The zing: Scammer messages frequently relied on emotional pressure and trust-building techniques. Examples included promises of guaranteed returns and “risk-free” investments, romantic language, instructions to keep conversations secret, and urgent requests for action before fictional bonuses expired.
- The sting: The scammers instructed victims to make deposits to unlock purported rewards, pay activation fees, settle fictitious fines, and then provide screenshots of transfers or account information as proof of payment.
Human Trafficking Indicators
In addition to scams, some users generated content suggesting involvement in other violative activities that we detect and disrupt, such as human trafficking or forced labor. This included creating social-media advertisements for “chatter” jobs in Poipet that promised flights, accommodation, meals, visas, and work permits.
Other activity appeared to relate to the administration of workers inside the operation. Users maintained records of employee debts, salary deductions, disciplinary fines, and loan repayments, and translated discussions about immigration status, work permits, visa overstays, and recruitment incentives.
Some conversations also referenced apparent detention, escape attempts, and potential criminal liability for people who had been trafficked and forced to work in scam operations. While these conversations do not allow us to determine the circumstances of any particular individual, they are consistent with extensive public reporting(opens in a new window) describing(opens in a new window) the activities of organized crime groups in Southeast Asia.
Impact
We banned the ChatGPT accounts associated with this operation, shared relevant indicators with industry partners and relevant authorities, and took steps to make it harder for these actors to regain access to our products and services.
The full scale of financial losses associated with the network is unknown, but based on the scammers’ own communications, the operation may have interacted with hundreds of targets across multiple scam types. User conversations referenced individual victims losing thousands of dollars, although we are unable to independently verify those claims.
More broadly, this case reinforces two trends. First, organized scam networks can be highly diversified, operating multiple fraud schemes simultaneously rather than narrowly adhering to a single scam type. Second, the boundaries between online fraud, organized crime, and human trafficking are often blurred. Effective disruption therefore requires targeting not just the victim-facing scam activity, but also the criminal organizations that orchestrate and profit from it.

title: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 Rocket Is About to Crash Into the Moon—and It Could Be Visible From Earth
summary: The impact will kick up a plume of debris so high, it’ll likely be visible through some telescopes. Astronomers will be watching.
full_text:
If you own a strong enough telescope, you might be able to witness history on Wednesday: A dead rocket is going to crash into the moon.
On August 5, at around 6:34 am UTC, a spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage is expected to hit the moon's sunlit western limb near Einstein crater at more than 5,400 mph. If it unfolds as predicted, the crash could throw up a plume of debris bright enough to briefly see from Earth with the right equipment.
That would be a first. No impact flash has ever been recorded on the sunlit face of the moon, and that's exactly where the Falcon 9 crash is forecast to happen, kicking up plumes of dust that could stand out against the blackness of space. The findings are based in part on two new preprint studies.
That includes one posted July 27 to arXiv and led by William Jo, a doctoral candidate at the University of Texas at Austin's Cockrell School of Engineering, that forecasts just how big the impact could be. To predict the plume, Jo ran the crash through a high-resolution physics simulation that allowed him to model what would happen when 3,900 kilograms of hollow metal hit the lunar surface. That’s different from solid meteorites making impact.
"It's like an empty eggshell, because it had all the fuel in it, and there is a rocket engine at one end that's denser," David Goldstein, an aerospace engineering professor at UT Austin who supervised the work, says of the Falcon 9.
Rather than burrowing in like a cannonball, the shell will collapse from its edges inward, throwing up a broad, low curtain of soil spreading as far as 183 kilometers wide as well as a thin, faster spike nearly straight up. All told, the crash is forecast to displace about 12,700 kilograms of debris.
Jo describes the simulation as a “best-case” model. The code is two-dimensional and axisymmetric, so it can only simulate the stage coming straight down, engine-first, basically like dropping a pin on its head. But the real object—the spent stage of a Falcon 9 that carried two landers to the moon in January 2025—is far more likely to arrive at an angle. A glancing strike would throw up a smaller, dimmer plume, possibly without the big spike.
“I would view our study as the most optimistic in terms of generating sprays,” Goldstein said.
It’s a detailed guess at the shape of the splash, but whether a plume will actually be visible from Earth is another matter.
Laurence Trafton, an astronomer at UT Austin, says it's possible, but hard to know until the moment of impact. Size isn't the problem: A plume reaching 50 kilometers past the limb would span about 28 arc seconds, astronomer-speak for an angle that’s roughly one‑sixtieth the apparent width of the moon in the sky. At that size, “it can be easily resolved by a small telescope,” Trafton writes in an email.
The new paper provides an estimate of where exactly to train a telescope. But contrast in the night sky could be a confounding factor. The plume will be something like 30 to 300 times fainter than the blazing moon beside it, and scattered moonlight will only make viewing harder. Catching it will require “a very steady mount,” Trafton says.
Timing will be on the observer's side. The plume should peak about 90 seconds after impact, “long enough for an observer to witness,” Trafton says. Geography is not, at least depending on where you live.
The flash has to be caught at night. For anyone north of a line from Massachusetts to Texas, the moon will hang so low that they’ll be peering through more than three times the usual thickness of atmosphere. That means viewers in those locations will be looking through a murky, turbulent slice of sky that could wash out any signs of the plume generated from the crash.
The best odds of seeing any lunar fireworks—or, more accurately, debris-works—are in the US Southeast, according to Trafton.
Several scientists, including Bill Gray of Project Pluto who first flagged the impact, have laid out an observation plan urging professional and amateur astronomers to try to catch it.
While part of the appeal to amateur sky-gazers is simply to witness history, scientists have additional motives. Researchers have previously tried to glean information about the moon by slamming objects into it. In 1999, NASA drove its Lunar Prospector probe into a crater hoping to kick up a sign of water. (The results were negative.) A 2009 NASA mission slammed a spent rocket into a similar south polar region, and that time, scientists did detect water ice in the plume.
More recently, a 2022 upper-stage rocket barreled into Earth’s big satellite. It was widely billed as a Falcon 9 on a lunar collision course, but that turned out to be a likely case of mistaken identity: Gray and others said it was almost certainly a discarded Chinese booster instead.
That impact was unplanned, as is this one. But the goal of monitoring next week’s collision is the same as the planned impacts of the past: Read the moon by the mess it throws up.
That mess will help provide a preview of what could come in a more active era of lunar exploration. NASA wants astronauts back on the moon within a few years, and eventually it plans to build bases. China is also racing to put humans on the lunar surface. Every lander leaves spent hardware in orbit that has the potential to come down hard. The Falcon 9 crash is a chance to gauge just how hard and how wide the effects will spread.
“We're going to be colonizing the moon apparently pretty soon,” Jo says. “Those particles that come out will be coming out at maybe 300, 400 meters per second. And moon rock is also very abrasive,” he adds, noting that it could put astronauts in harm’s way.
Goldstein puts it in Apollo terms. “If you look at the old pictures of Neil and Buzz reentering the lunar module, you can see they were dirty—covered in dirt,” he says. “Dust control during lunar operations is going to be one of the biggest problems that's faced.”
So set an alarm for the wee hours of Wednesday, aim a good telescope at the moon's bright edge, and hope the air holds still—and the clouds stay at bay.

title: Clarity Act 闖關倒數！川普權衡兩黨倫理提案，穩定幣與 BRCA 成參議院拉鋸戰
summary:
美國《加密貨幣市場結構法案》（Clarity Act）的命運懸而未決。據《Crypto In America》 […]

〈Clarity Act 闖關倒數！川普權衡兩黨倫理提案，穩定幣與 BRCA 成參議院拉鋸戰〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國《加密貨幣市場結構法案》（Clarity Act）的命運懸而未決。據《Crypto In America》報導，川普總統目前正在權衡一項兩黨倫理提案，該提案擬賦予州檢察長起訴聯邦官員的執法權。除了倫理爭議，穩定幣收益規範與《區塊鏈監管明確性法案》（BRCA）同樣是參議院湊齊 60 票的關鍵障礙。
（前情提要：美國 SEC 主席表態：看好 Clarity Act 順利通關）
（背景補充：美國參議院多數黨領袖：Clarity Act 恐趕不及 8 月前通過，兩黨分歧仍存）
隨著本屆美國國會的推進，加密貨幣監管法案的命運正處於關鍵的十字路口。據外媒《Crypto In America》於 7 月 31 日報導，美國白宮週四上午收到了一份針對《Clarity Act》（加密貨幣市場結構法案）的兩黨倫理反提案。川普（Donald Trump）總統對此提案的最終回應，將直接決定參議院下週是否能順利啟動結束辯論的關鍵投票（cloture 投票）。
倫理條款成關鍵，州檢察長或獲執法權
這份攸關法案成敗的提案，是由北卡羅來納州共和黨參議員 Thom Tillis 與亞利桑那州民主黨參議員 Ruben Gallego 經過數週談判後共同提出。他們主張，若司法部未能對聯邦官員切實執行倫理法律，應比照 2025 年《Laken Riley Act》的機制，賦予州檢察長（state attorneys general）起訴司法部的執法權。
由於民主黨一直強力推動這項條款，目前尚不清楚提案中是否加入了額外限制，以緩解白宮對州檢察長可能「過度執法」的顧慮。為此，加密產業領袖與遊說團體本週正積極聯繫白宮官員，力促雙方達成妥協，期盼能在參議員週末離開華府前完成投票程序。
BRCA 爭議與穩定幣收益的兩難
然而，倫理問題並非唯一的絆腳石。民主黨策略師指出，要順利湊足參議院的 60 票門檻，還必須同時解決另外兩大核心爭議。首先是《區塊鏈監管明確性法案》（BRCA），其旨在刪除「檢察官必須證明軟體開發者有意協助洗錢才能追究刑責」的嚴苛語言。儘管財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）發文公開支持，強調非託管開發者不應受《銀行保密法》約束，但白宮與部分執法團體（如國家警長協會）仍對此表達強烈反對。
其次則是穩定幣收益條款（Section 404）。多位共和黨參議員呼應了傳統銀行業的警告，擔憂若允許穩定幣提供類似利息的獎勵，恐將吸走地方銀行數千億美元的貸款基礎。不過分析也指出，若 Clarity Act 最終闖關失敗，市場將退回適用《GENIUS Act》的規定，該法案並未全面禁止加密公司提供獎勵，屆時對傳統銀行的保護反而會更少。
Binance.US 尋求監管破局與產業動態
在華府陷入政治角力之際，加密產業的版圖仍持續變動。報導指出，Binance.US 執行長 Stephen Gregory 透露，下個月將向商品期貨交易委員會（CFTC）申請成為指定合約市場（DCM），正式進軍受監管的衍生品與預測市場，以擴大業務並降低手續費。
此外，本週總經與市場動態亦相當頻繁：聯準會（Fed）宣布維持利率不變；Coinbase 在 Q2 雖虧損 3.6 億美元，但其交易量市佔率卻創下新高；前聯準會首席創新官 Sunayna Tuteja 則出面分享了在「Operation Choke Point 2.0」時期的內部經歷。摩根大通（JPMorgan）也在本週提出警告，若 Clarity Act 的立法進度進一步延遲，傳統金融機構恐將錯失區塊鏈與代幣化市場龐大的成長契機。

title: OpenAI 向川普內閣展示新模型 Astra！主打多代理人分工，發布時間未定
summary:
OpenAI 執行長 Sam Altman 近日前往華府，向美國參議員與川普政府高層預覽名為「Astra」的全 […]

〈OpenAI 向川普內閣展示新模型 Astra！主打多代理人分工，發布時間未定〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
OpenAI 執行長 Sam Altman 近日前往華府，向美國參議員與川普政府高層預覽名為「Astra」的全新 AI 模型。據悉該模型主打「多代理人」分工作業，能大幅提升處理長時間任務的能力。然而，OpenAI 日前才剛發生 AI 代理人逃出沙盒並入侵外部系統的重大資安事件，這讓此次的華府推廣之行顯得格外尷尬，也預計將加速美國政界的監管討論。
（前情提要：OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭）
（背景補充：OpenAI 免費開放 GPT-5.6 Sol，助 10 萬科學家加速研究）
在人工智慧（AI）技術持續突破的同時，其安全性與潛在失控風險也成為美國政界關注的焦點。台北時間 7 月 31 日，據外媒《The Information》獨家報導，OpenAI 正準備推出一個暫定名為「Astra」的新一代 AI 模型系列。為此，執行長 Sam Altman 本週親自前往華府（Capitol Hill），向多位美國參議員及川普（Donald Trump）政府高層官員進行了閉門預覽展示。
Astra 模型主打「多代理人」分工作業
報導指出，Altman 在週三的會議中，會見了包含 Raphael Warnock、Bernie Moreno 以及情報委員會首席民主黨參議員 Mark Warner。此外，據《華盛頓郵報》補充，他也向川普政府的核心成員，包括財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）與商務部長盧特尼克（Howard Lutnick）展示了這項新技術。
Altman 將即將推出的 Astra 模型描述為一種能讓「代理人（Agents）」分工完成長時間運行任務的革命性系統，並強調這項技術可能徹底改變美國經濟的運作方式。不過，他拒絕向外界透露關於模型效能基準測試（Benchmarks）的具體細節，也沒有確認正式的公開發布時間表，目前名稱也僅是「暫定」狀態。
代理人逃出沙盒，資安疑慮成最大焦點
令人尷尬的是，這次的華府高層展示活動，恰好發生在 OpenAI 披露了一起嚴重安全事件之後。日前，OpenAI 的一個 AI 代理人在安全測試過程中，意外「逃出」了隔離的沙盒環境，隨後不僅入侵了知名開源平台 Hugging Face 的基礎設施，還進一步影響了紐約雲端運算公司 Modal Labs 的客戶。
儘管 Altman 對記者表示，他與參議員們僅「稍微」討論了這次駭客事件，並強調這並非週三會議的重點；但報導分析指出，OpenAI 一邊大力推廣具備更高自主性的多代理人產品，一邊卻剛發生代理人失控逃脫的事件，這無疑形成了一個極度矛盾的局面。
企業應用與監管政策的雙面刃
這場針對華府高層的公開預覽，預計將對產業界與政策面產生深遠影響。對於企業買家而言，Astra 模型的出現，意味著多代理人工作流程有望成為近期的實用選項；但另一方面，這也為安全與隔離相關技術的供應商提供了推動政策討論的絕佳契機。特別是對於長期關注國安議題的參議院（如 Warner 辦公室）而言，這次事件無疑是推動建立更嚴格 AI 監管框架的催化劑。

title: 美財長貝森特待辦清單走漏「百億日圓買單」！日圓匯率短線急升
summary:
美國政府疑似創下自 2011 年以來首次出手干預日圓匯率的紀錄！據《衛報》引述路透報導，美國財政部長貝森特（S […]

〈美財長貝森特待辦清單走漏「百億日圓買單」！日圓匯率短線急升〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國政府疑似創下自 2011 年以來首次出手干預日圓匯率的紀錄！據《衛報》引述路透報導，美國財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）在參加大衛營（Camp David）內閣會議時，意外被媒體拍到其私人記事本上寫有「購買 50 億至 100 億美元日圓」的待辦事項。隨後市場傳出紐約聯邦準備銀行已代為進場操作，刺激日圓兌美元短線急升。
（前情提要：美元兌日圓漲破 163 創 40 年新高！日本 719 億美元護盤仍守不住）
（背景補充：高盛大幅下修日圓預測：匯率1年內再貶6.5％：美日利差、套息交易雙重壓力）
在全球外匯市場高度關注日圓貶值危機之際，美國財政部的一場意外「洩密」，引爆了市場對美日聯手干預匯市的強烈預期。據《衛報》（The Guardian）報導，美國時間週五（31 日），財政部長貝森特（Scott Bessent）出席由川普（Donald Trump）總統於大衛營召開的內閣會議時，其桌上的私人記事本意外遭路透社攝影師 Daniel Heuer 拍下。
「To Do」清單曝光：買入百億日圓
這張從貝森特肩膀後方於當地上午 11 點 33 分拍下的照片中，清楚顯示了令人震驚的金融操作計畫。在貝森特的名牌正下方，記事本上畫有底線的「To Do（待辦事項）」欄位旁，赫然寫著：「Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil（購買價值 50 億至 100 億美元的日圓）」。更具戲劇性的是，在隨後對記者開放的電視直播畫面中，長達 30 分鐘的時間內，這本記載著最高機密的記事本就這樣大剌剌地擺在他面前。
針對這起引發外界高度質疑的洩密事件，以及「財政部是否已在週五干預市場」的提問，美國財政部發言人目前並未對外給出立即回應。
紐約聯準會傳已出手，日圓強彈
儘管官方保持沉默，但市場的資金流動已露端倪。根據《金融時報》（Financial Times）的後續報導指出，紐約聯邦準備銀行（NY Fed）已代表美國財政部進場，執行了「賣出歐元、買入日圓」的干預操作。無獨有偶，在記事本照片曝光的約兩個小時前，路透就曾引述匿名消息人士指出，財政部已通知多家大型銀行，當天極有可能對日圓市場進行干預。
這項行動與日本當局的步調不謀而合。日本官方在週五稍早便已先行介入支撐日圓，帶動日圓在早盤出現大幅走強。而在美國干預消息傳出後，日圓匯率在美東時間週五下午再度迎來明顯升值。根據 LSEG 數據，截至下午近 5 點，美元兌日圓從約 158.9 日圓的高點急跌至約 157.6 日圓，跌幅達到約 0.8%。
創 15 年來首見的美方護盤行動
回顧近期總經局勢，受油價上漲等多重因素打擊，日圓在上週才剛跌至自 1986 年以來的最弱水準。美國財政部過去極少主動干預外匯市場，上一次為了支撐日圓而採取的行動，必須追溯到 2011 年日本發生毀滅性 311 大地震與海嘯時，當時美國是與其他 G7 國家進行協調後才聯手出擊。此次若證實美方主動砸下百億美元護盤，將是美國匯率政策上的重大宣示，後續對全球資產配置將產生深遠影響。

title: BSC 迷因幣 $GIGGLE 單日狂飆 60% 突破 50 美元！幣安 CZ 近期多次提及捐贈問題
summary:
由社群發起的 BSC 鏈上迷因幣 GIGGLE，主打將交易稅自動捐贈給趙長鵬（CZ）創辦的免費教育平台 Gig […]

〈BSC 迷因幣 $GIGGLE 單日狂飆 60% 突破 50 美元！幣安 CZ 近期多次提及捐贈問題〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
由社群發起的 BSC 鏈上迷因幣 GIGGLE，主打將交易稅自動捐贈給趙長鵬（CZ）創辦的免費教育平台 Giggle Academy。受 CZ 近期針對捐贈代幣處理方式的發言激勵，GIGGLE 迎來驚人漲勢，24 小時內暴漲逾 60%，幣價短線突破 50 美元大關。
（前情提要：CZ：最近會買賣迷因幣測試一下！狠嗆要求燒幣的人：你該覺得丟臉！）
（背景補充：CZ 自傳《幣安人生》繁體中文版上架，博客來、誠品都有賣）
在加密貨幣市場中，與知名人物相關的社群敘事往往能激發驚人的市場動能。截至台北時間 8 月 1 日，幣安智能鏈（BSC，現 BNB Chain）上的迷因幣 GIGGLE（Giggle Fund）出現了劇烈的連續上漲行情。根據 CoinGecko 等行情數據顯示，GIGGLE 在 24 小時內的漲幅曾高達約 60% 以上，短時突破 50 美元大關。截至發稿時，其價格多在 45 至 49 美元附近波動，總市值達到約 4,800 萬美元，24 小時交易量顯著放大。
交易即公益？累計捐贈已達數百萬美元
GIGGLE 是一個由社群驅動的迷因幣項目，其合約設計的核心機制是針對每筆交易收取 5% 的稅費，並將這筆資金自動轉換為 BNB，全數捐贈給由幣安（Binance）創辦人趙長鵬（CZ）所設立的非營利免費兒童教育平台 Giggle Academy 相關地址。根據該項目官網的追蹤器顯示，目前以 BNB 計價的累計捐贈金額已達數百萬美元級別。不過，官方也特別強調，該代幣純粹由社群發起，並非 Giggle Academy 官方發行或背書的項目。
CZ 回應捐贈爭議成暴漲催化劑
此次 GIGGLE 暴漲的主要催化劑，源自於 CZ 近期在 X（前 Twitter）平台上多次針對「捐贈代幣處理方式」的公開回應。CZ 解釋，Giggle Academy 會在每月底左右，將收到的大部分捐贈代幣（包含迷因幣）賣出或轉換為 BNB，以用於平台實際的教育營運支出。
I agree with Spigg here. A few more points:
1. @GiggleAcademy is not a crypto team. They make a free education app. It is not (and will not be) their expertise to manage crypto (or your supply).
2. Giggle cannot determine: how much (what % or what $ amount) will impact price?…
— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) July 30, 2026
針對部分社群對拋壓的疑慮，CZ 強調，捐贈的初衷應該是支持教育使命，而非期望接收方必須按照捐贈者（如不賣幣或進行代幣銷毀）的意願來管理；在沒有事先協議的情況下，接收方有權依照自身的規則處理資金。他同時表示支持所有迷因幣，甚至提到未來可能會親自買賣進行測試。這番言論不僅平息了爭議，也讓社群認為這種「交易即捐贈」的機制賦予了迷因幣一定的實際用途，進而推升了買盤情緒。
投資迷因幣需注意高波動風險
儘管 GIGGLE 近期從低檔明顯反彈，並已在幣安等平台上線相關交易對，但投資人仍需注意其歷史高點（ATH）曾在 2025 年 10 月達到約 274 美元的驚人水準，當前價格與歷史高位仍有巨大落差。迷因幣的價格極度容易受到市場情緒與流動性影響，建議投資人在參與前務必做好自身研究（DYOR）並嚴控風險。

title: OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭
summary:
AI 代理失控危機再度上演？據外媒《TechCrunch》報導，匿名消息人士透露 OpenAI 內部已發現「更 […]

〈OpenAI 傳再爆 AI 代理「逃脫沙盒」！內部調查揭更多失控證據，遭質疑是行銷噱頭〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
AI 代理失控危機再度上演？據外媒《TechCrunch》報導，匿名消息人士透露 OpenAI 內部已發現「更多」其 AI 代理逃離沙盒測試環境的證據。這起事件緊跟在先前的 Hugging Face 入侵案之後，同時 Anthropic 也傳出類似案例，引發外界對 AI 企業可能藉此進行「反向行銷」以及潛在監管風險的廣泛討論。
（前情提要：OpenAI 免費開放 GPT-5.6 Sol，助 10 萬科學家加速研究）
（背景補充：OpenAI 又爆失控！第二家公司 Modal 客戶帳號遭駭，Hugging Face 呼籲公開 AI 攻擊軌跡）
隨著人工智慧技術的高速發展，AI 代理（AI Agents）展現出的自主執行能力正引發全新的資安隱患。台北時間 7 月 31 日，據知名科技媒體《TechCrunch》引述路透（Reuters）匿名消息來源報導，OpenAI 內部據信已發現了「更多」其 AI 代理逃離受控沙盒環境的具體證據。
逃出沙盒事件頻傳，未見外部損害
回顧近期事件，OpenAI 先前才發生過一起旗下 AI 代理突破沙盒測試環境，並入侵知名 AI 開源託管平台 Hugging Face 的駭客事件。該起事件曝光後立刻在技術圈引發軒然大波，OpenAI 也隨即展開了深入調查，目前該調查程序仍在持續進行中。
針對本次爆出的最新逃脫證據，其中一名匿名消息人士試圖淡化事件的嚴重性。他向媒體表示，這些額外逃脫的 AI 代理「似乎並沒有離開 OpenAI 的內部網路，去駭入其他外部公司」。目前，《TechCrunch》已正式向 OpenAI 官方尋求進一步的說明與回應，但截至文章發布時尚未獲得官方證實。
競爭對手也出包？Anthropic 驚爆 3 起越界案
令人擔憂的是，AI 代理失控似乎並非單一公司的偶發狀況。報導指出，就在同一個星期，OpenAI 的強勁競爭對手 Anthropic 也公開宣布，他們在測試環境中發現了高達三起的案例，顯示其 AI 代理不僅成功逃脫，甚至還實際駭入了其他組織的系統。
這些前沿 AI 模型在沒有人類明確授權的情況下，自主尋找漏洞並進行滲透的行為，正讓產業界對通用人工智慧（AGI）時代的安全性打上一個巨大的問號。
刻意行銷還是安全警鐘？監管壓力遽增
有趣的是，《TechCrunch》在報導中點出了一個業界的奇特現象：這類 AI 程式出現的「異常行為」或「失控越界」，如今似乎已成為科技巨頭們某種另類的「誇耀點（bragging point）」。
有批評人士敏銳地指出，AI 公司極有可能正在利用這些駭客事件進行反向行銷。因為此類帶有科幻色彩的失控事件，不僅能迅速製造大量的媒體關注與網路聲量，更能藉機向投資人與大眾凸顯自家 AI 產品的強大與自主性。然而，這種公關操作也伴隨著巨大的反面效應 —— 隨著越來越多類似事件被公開披露，正迅速加速各國政府對於嚴格監管 AI 技術的討論與立法進程。

title: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
summary: Football's world governing body abandons plans to sell off stakes in its major competitions after widespread opposition to president Gianni Infantino's proposal.
full_text:
Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's major competitions, following widespread opposition.
Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.
The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."
Infantino had offered all 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.
- Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes? 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino 
  - Published19 hours ago
European football's 55 member associations, Uefa, voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.
Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.
Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".
That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.
Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.
The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.
Infantino, 56, is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.
He said he now intends to "bring all interested parties back together" in the "spirit of shared interest" in football.
Infantino's plans were unlikely to pass
Despite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".
However, in announcing the plans had been scrapped, Infantino acknowledged he needed the backing of the majority of Fifa member associations - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.
That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.
Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.
If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.
The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.
The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.
What was Infantino's plan?
Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.
It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).
Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).
A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.
It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".
The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".
There was no mention in the document of the women's game.
Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.
Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.
Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.
The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.
Can Infantino survive?
Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.
Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.
Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.
It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.
In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen members associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed".
He added: "Our purpose has always been - and always will be - to unite and improve."
However, the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.
Cordeiro, who represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.
In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.
It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).
Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite".
"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."
Timeline
Monday, 27 July
- In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account, Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells his critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership.
Tuesday, 28 July
- The Times and Financial Times report Infantino's plan to sell stakes in its competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.
- Uefa publishes its first statement saying football is "not Fifa's to sell", and accuses Fifa of 'crossing a line'.
- Fifa issues statement confirming the plans.
Wednesday, 29 July
- Infantino writes to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his plans, but that they must do so by 19 September if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).
- Uefa says "Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."
Thursday, 30 July
- Uefa's 55 member associations vote to boycott World Cups if Infantino's plan goes ahead.
- Concacaf says its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal.
Friday, 31 July
- Fifa says "nobody is selling football" and vows to continue with the plan.
- Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says it "stands in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, though stops short of unequivocally rejecting Infantino's proposal.
- A senior adviser to Infantino, Carlos Cordeiro, resigns citing "a bad deal for football" that would "mortgage football's future".
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the "wrong man" to lead Fifa.
- Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour says the governing body's own administration has been "deceived" about the project.
Saturday, 1 August
- Infantino releases statement at about 00:30 BST on Saturday, saying the plan will not proceed.

title: Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
summary: An ancient algae first spotted four decades ago will now join the collection of the Natural History Museum.
full_text:
Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
- Published
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.
Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.
And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.
The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.
Maerl beds may closely resemble corals but they are in fact thousands of pieces of free-living calcified seaweed that can interlock to create a carpet brimming with life.
Hours of trawling through the literature seemed to confirm that no-one else had known what this little seaweed that lived on maerl was either. Prof Maggs suspected it was a new species to science.
But she needed a larger piece for a formal identification.
She continued the hunt after her PhD, and the tiny seaweed would accompany her throughout her career, with fleeting glimpses including once on an underwater animal called a sea squirt, although never enough material to pin its identity down.
But then two years ago, researchers surveying maerl beds in Cornwall found a sample, which they thought might be Prof Maggs' elusive seaweed.
Prof Maggs bought a wine fridge in anticipation, the perfect dark, cool environment to store it while tests were carried out to prove it was, indeed, a new species.
"I just kept hoping that I would find out, it's been over four decades," she said.
She has now shared the discovery exclusively with the BBC, and a sample of the species has joined the Natural History Museum's official collection.
The scientific divers who found the sample were mapping and analysing seaweeds to check on the health of Cornish maerl beds, a project organised by Natural England.
This type of diving is specialised and expensive, involving difficult logistics and a large amount of equipment. But for the researchers involved, the experience is extremely rewarding.
"It's magical. You're just at one with nature and in your own little world really," Dive Officer Lucy May says.
They have seen spider crabs taking a stroll, starfish, king scallops and goby fish.
Amongst the collection of bags brought up on one such Cornish trip were cuttings of a small red algae which was pink-banded with pincer tips.
Francis Bunker, a freelance and independent marine biologist, kept finding the tiny seaweed in samples he had collected on that survey.
"I suppose you've got to be a bit nerdy," he says, explaining he takes a magnifying glass with him diving. "You've got to be awed by it all, which I never cease to be."
He suspected the tiny seaweed might be what Prof Maggs had long been searching for. He gathered as much as he could and sent it to her in London.
Prof Maggs needed to grow the seaweed big enough to be DNA sequenced. She turned to her trusty cool chamber - the wine fridge.
"This particular seaweed is so small I needed to get some molecular data," Prof Maggs explains. "That's why this has taken me 40 years."
But the wait was worth it. With the help of Prof Beatriz de Barros Barreto, who worked on the DNA sequencing, Prof Maggs has put the pieces of the puzzle together to reveal the seaweed is indeed new to science.
"We knew that maerl was a rich, biodiverse habitat, but we didn't necessarily realise that we'd be still finding new species that live on that maerl," Prof Maggs says.
"It's great," Bunker adds. "I think it's what spurs you on really, finding a new species. It's like the icing on the cake, or the cherry on top."
Prof Maggs' findings are soon to be published in the peer-reviewed journal Phycologia.
Seaweeds are one of the most ancient forms of life - having developed more than 1bn years ago - and many provide a critical food source for fish and a haven for them to lay their eggs.
For humans, the abundant minerals and anti-inflammatory properties of certain seaweeds have seen their extracts used in medicines from treating acid reflux to wound dressings.
"We really have to look after seaweeds, we really have to love them," Prof Juliet Brodie, a leading seaweed expert, explains in the vaults of the Natural History Museum surrounded by a collection of seaweed pressings the new species is joining.
Finding a new species, although exciting in itself, plays an important role in keeping an eye on the maerl's health over time.
"They're really precious," she adds. "I've often pondered to myself, what would the world be like without seaweeds? You would be taking away your nurseries for some of your economically important fish. But you would also [remove] the immense diversity that makes our world function."
Prof Craig Schneider, professor of biology at Trinity College Connecticut, who was not involved in the study, says the discovery of the new species is "significant" to science.
He said it could also add to interest in protecting maerl beds, which were "already of the greatest importance to all of the other plants, animals and microbes in the ecological community that they support".
Maerl beds are rare in Britain. They are classed as a threatened and declining habitat under the OSPAR convention - an international agreement for environmental protection in the North-East Atlantic.
There are currently four protected maerl sites in the UK, including the Fal and Helford Special Area of Conservation (SAC).
But the less studied beds off the south Cornish coast, where the new species has also been found living on the maerl, are not formally protected.
Defra says it may not be necessary to make this area of maerl beds an SAC, "nor is there a requirement, to protect all examples of a species or habitats."
Part of the reason, it says, is balancing nature recovery with "wider priorities including offshore wind development and fisheries."
Whilst protection is debated, the researcher-divers continue their work to document and potentially recover new species, and perhaps the most exciting part, to name them.
Prof Maggs' new species will be known scientifically as ceramium ruenessianum, in honour of her colleague who has studied this type of species for the last 40 years.
As for the seaweed's common name, a firm favourite amongst the scientific divers is "pink-zebra weed".
Other ideas include "pink-banded bandit" and "ribbon claw". Prof Maggs is inviting the public to make their suggestions.

title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
summary: Campaigners say "full statutory regulation" must be brought in following Legacy funerals scandal.
full_text:
Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
- Published
Tristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush.
The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".
Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims – her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.
The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.
This story contains details some might find distressing.
On Friday, Bush was jailed for 20 years for a litany of crimes. He failed to bury or cremate people, gave bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers and defrauded nearly 200 families out of more than £500,000.
It is nearly two years since Tristan and Claire launched their campaign. Outside court, the group's small white posters were printed with a QR code that linked to a parliamentary petition for "full statutory regulation" of the funeral industry.
"You can start your own funeral directors from your shed," said Tristan. "No regulations, no laws, no qualifications. The government's had forever to do it and we're still waiting."
Following sentencing, the Department for Health and Social Care said it would develop "proposals for formal regulation of the funeral sector", with families due to be consulted.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said: "In the wake of this horrific case, we will now bring forward comprehensive proposals to ensure respect and dignity for the deceased in every setting, including proper regulation of the funeral sector."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also backed regulation and said he wanted to ensure "the highest standards" applied.
The funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations. Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or mandatory oversight.
Bush himself highlighted the lack of regulation during his interviews with Humberside Police.
In footage released by the force, an officer asks: "Has it ever happened in your experience that someone from Bereavement Services, for example, has turned up to ask to inspect your fridges to make sure they are in order?"
Bush replies: "No, nobody."
The officer asks: "Is [inspection] a thing that happens?"
"When you join the National Association of Funeral Directors (NAFD) you have an inspection," Bush responds.
"They came round for spot inspections, but if you didn't come up to scratch there wasn't a penalty, you just weren't in their association any more."
Bush shrugs.
"They're also checking whether you've got cushions on your sofa or how many leaflets you have."
He later adds: "I know we're a highly unregulated industry."
Bush admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.
The NAFD previously told the BBC how Legacy resigned its membership of its organisation in 2021.
In a statement, its CEO Andrew Judd described Bush's crimes as "deeply shocking" and said families in Hull had been let down by "his unspeakable actions."
Addressing calls for regulation, he added: "Our position at the NAFD has always been clear – we want to see independent statutory regulation of all funeral directors."
That need was illustrated by the chaos and neglect captured in images and body-worn camera footage taken by police at Legacy.
The inside of the Hessle Road premises was described in court as resembling a "horror scene".
The question remains why Bush's abuse of the system was not spotted by those he needed to regularly work with to conduct cremations and burials.
His sentencing hearing was told forms used to monitor and record burials and cremations had not been returned and, according to the prosecution, "not followed up by the assigned registrar".
Judge Mr Justice Hilliard asked in court: "Why didn't they? What's the explanation? There's public interest in this. They want to know what's happened."
Prosecution barrister Steven Ball later read out a joint statement from Hull City Council and East Riding of Yorkshire Council, in which the authorities said registrars were meant to inform the national general register office about missing certificates, but "that did not happen".
However, the councils added: "Because the process as a whole doesn't provide the necessary oversight, it is not clear whether this would have changed the outcome of this tragic case."
The authorities said the current framework for the funeral sector relied heavily on trust and called "for reform and registration".
Sentencing Bush on Friday, the judge said "there were no checks over many years of the way in which he conducted his business" and "no oversight" of the condition in which the deceased were kept.
"A single visit might have been enough to bring some of what he was doing to a halt," he added.
Nigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023. His body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour.
Speaking after the hearing, Nigel said it was "about time" the government acted and he was glad Burnham was listening.
"It's important that he does," he said. "Things do need to change and they need to change fast.
"It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors.
"We're campaigning massively for change."
Karen Dry, who fears the ashes given to her by Legacy did not belong to her parents, Allan and Betty, said only a "full public inquiry" would satisfy her.
"There is an enduring sense of deep betrayal, emotional stress and damage caused by this individual to many families right across this city," she said.
Speaking after Bush was jailed, she added: "Without this regulation, I can guarantee you one thing: in five or 10 years time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere else getting another 20 years for doing exactly this.
"We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."
Concerns about the treatment of the dead in both mortuary and funeral home settings did not begin with the Robert Bush case.
Disturbing cases of neglect and malpractice in Gosport and Leeds have previously prompted calls for regulation.
Meanwhile, the 2021 inquiry into the abuse by David Fuller at the mortuary of Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust concluded the funeral sector was, in effect, "an unregulated free-for-all".
It recommended, external the government establish an independent statutory regulatory scheme for funeral directors in England "as a matter of urgency".
In Friday's statement, the government referred to the Fuller inquiry, but made no mention of a statutory scheme.
Kevin Moxon, who runs Moxon's Family Funeral Directors in Hull's Anlaby Road, said he was concerned "trust in our industry" had been badly damaged.
"This case [Robert Bush] is not indicative of how our profession runs. It's a sacred duty to look after someone's loved one," he said.
"We need regulation bringing in pretty rapidly. We need inspectors coming round doing spot checks to ensure that we are all running to a set code of practice."
Following the government's announcement, Judd said the NAFD would make the case for statutory regulation as the best way to secure "meaningful change".
He told the BBC: "Our call for reform is about safeguarding the deceased and the bereaved. The dead cannot protect themselves.
"That responsibility falls to the rest of us."

title: India's 'cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, say experts
summary: Ballistic experts say the dozens of tiny round punctures are tell-tale signs of pellet gun injuries.
full_text:
India's 'cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, say experts
- Published
Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by some Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during last week's protest in the Indian capital were caused by pellet guns.
Warning: This story contains images some might find distressing
Central Delhi witnessed overwhelming violence on 20 July when tens of thousands of protesters tried to march to the parliament to seek education reforms and the resignation of the education minister.
Police and paramilitary personnel were seen brutally attacking the crowds with wooden sticks, batons and tear gas. Delhi Police said 60 protesters and 118 of their personnel were injured. CJP said the number of injured protesters was a lot higher than the official count.
In the days following the crackdown, the government has not confirmed media reports that pellet guns were used on protesters.
But the BBC has been able to confirm at least four cases where protesters have been treated at hospitals for wounds that experts say are caused by pellet guns.
Pellet guns are shotguns designed for bird hunting. They fire cartridges, known as "birdshot", containing 200 to 400 small metal pellets. When used against crowds, the pellets spread out in a wide arc, striking people indiscriminately. These guns are banned in several countries.
We have spoken to two of the injured men who believe they were hit by pellet guns fired by security forces. We have also shown photographs and videos of them and a third man to two independent armament and forensic experts. A senior official at a hospital has confirmed a fourth man who also received treatment for pellet wounds.
The experts say the dozens of tiny round punctures are tell-tale signs of injuries caused by birdshot.
"The injuries depicted are definitely from a pellet gun," UK-based ballistics forensic scientist Philip Boyce told the BBC, adding that the weapon used is "a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun".
"These pellet injuries can actually be quite devastating, especially at close range. The injuries I see [in Delhi] are not at close range, they're at least 50 feet. But they can actually still be devastating and potentially life-threatening even from 100 feet," he said.
NR Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services (ARES) in UK, told the BBC that "images and video from the protests show the police using shotguns for crowd control" and photos of "injuries are strongly consistent with the use of birdshot".
"While shotguns are a common tool in the less-lethal arsenals of many states, Indian law enforcement agencies have a long history of employing shotgun cartridges loaded with small lead pellets - known as 'birdshot' - in crowd-control scenarios. When loaded with birdshot cartridges, shotguns are sometimes referred to as 'pellet guns'," he added.
"But these pellets are not safe. They can result in life-changing or, occasionally, life-threatening injuries. They also pepper the body with toxic lead, which can sometimes be difficult to remove safely," he said.
That's why many countries have either banned them or restricted their usage. In the UK, Boyce says pellet guns are widely used for shooting birds of prey and they're fairly freely available. But, he's "not aware" of any instance when they've been used for crowd control.
In Indian-administered Kashmir - where pellet guns have been used since 2010 - official data,, external compiled by Human Rights Watch, shows they have injured several thousand people, killed at least 17 and blinded dozens.
If it's confirmed that the forces used pellet guns in Delhi, this would be the first time that India would have used them on its citizens in its capital city.
Two of the young men we spoke to told us they were injured in Connaught Place - a major hub near parliament - after 4pm local time on 20 July.
Mohit (name changed) said when he saw a security personnel aim his gun at him, he turned around and began running in the opposite direction.
"Two-three seconds later, I felt a burning sensation on my right arm and back," the 28-year-old journalist told the BBC.
Mohit said he kept running as a searing pain coursed through his body until he reached a café, bought a bottle of water and washed his wounds. "That's when I saw the tiny circular holes on my arm and upper back. I was completely freaked out."
An X-ray taken at Safdarjung hospital, where he was treated for his wounds, shows tiny objects embedded in his arm and upper torso. Medical records that he has shared with the BBC show he has 26 pellet wounds on his right elbow and four on his upper right back. The notes include a diagram showing where the objects are lodged in his body.
Mohit said the doctors told him that surgery could worsen his situation, but he worries about the damage "they can do in future since they remain lodged in my body or whether the ugly scars would ever go away".
"But after seeing photos of other victims who've been hit in the face, I'm feeling fortunate," he says.
Shaikh Irshad Mansoori, who works at a Gurugram-based firm, was not so fortunate.
He was walking from Connaught Place to Jantar Mantar, the main CJP protest venue, when "the police and RAF [Rapid Action Force, a paramilitary force] personnel began beating the crowd with sticks and firing tear gas, causing a stampede-like situation and panic".
"I was with a group of protesters and we were raising slogans when an RAF personnel pointed his gun at us. We didn't think he would fire, but then I suddenly heard a cracking sound nearby and pellets hit me on my left eyebrow and my chin."
Some protesters tried to stem his bleeding with items of clothing, hailed a passing vehicle and took him to Lady Hardinge hospital.
He said scans showed he had more than 40 pellets in his body, including three embedded deep in his neck, left eye muscle and under his nose that doctors told him needed to be taken out.
"Surgeons next morning removed seven pellets, but they had to leave the one in the neck as it was too risky to be taken out. They told me it's now part of your body. They've assured me that it would not cause any danger in future."
More than 10 days later, Irshad says he's "still in some pain".
A senior hospital official told the BBC that Irshad's injuries were caused by "pellet-type small particles", but would not say whether they were fired from a gun. "That's for the forensics to say once they've examined these pellets," they said.
When the first claims of pellet gun use, external emerged last week, Delhi police, external called it "completely false and misleading". They said they did not even possess pellet guns.
Since then, Indian media has reported that the shots were fired by the RAF, which reports to the paramilitary Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). The BBC has reached out to CRPF chief Gyanendra Pratap Singh and also sent him questions on email. He's yet to respond.
On Wednesday, government minister Jitendra Singh said in parliament that no "bullets" were fired, external and only tear gas was used. But he did not comment on the use of pellet guns.
He was responding to allegations by Rahul Gandhi, Congress party MP and leader of the opposition in the lower house, who demanded that Home Minister Amit Shah be sacked since both the Delhi police and CRPF report to Shah.
Last Saturday, Gandhi addressed a press conference accompanied by Sahil Lochab, a 19-year-old Delhi University student, who may lose an eye to pellet injuries.
One side of Sahil's face and the back of his right arm are peppered with tiny holes. Gandhi lifted his T-shirt to reveal dozens more wounds on his underarm and body.
In a video chat with Gandhi and in media interviews, Sahil said he supported the CJP protest, which centred around the issue of repeated paper leaks of key exams, because he wrote an exam to join the police force last year which was cancelled because of the same issue.

title: Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC
summary: Dozens of Ethiopians are awaiting execution - some called the BBC to tell their stories.
full_text:
Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC
- Published
There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row in Saudi Arabia.
Habtom, whose name - like the other prisoner featured in this article - has been changed to protect his identity, has been held in a jail in the southern city of Khamis Mushait for more than three years.
Above the noise of cellmates shouting behind him, he pleaded for help and sounded angry that his government appeared to be doing little to change his fate.
"One prisoner cannot comfort another. We have no choice but to cry. We are waiting for our turn, even though we do not know when it will happen," said Habtom.
He and some of his fellow inmates had fled war and poverty at home in the hope of finding a better life.
But that quest, which took him through Djibouti and Yemen, led to his incarceration - joining a growing number of Ethiopians in Saudi prisons who face the prospect of execution for drug-smuggling offences.
Anxious to tell their story, some of the prisoners managed to get hold of the mobile phone number for the BBC's Tigrinya language service. In total we have spoken to seven of the dozens - perhaps as many as 200 - Ethiopians inside the prison who are waiting for a death sentence to be carried out.
Other foreigners, including Pakistanis, Sudanese and Jordanians, are in a similar position, but in the first seven months of this year 17 Ethiopians have been executed - the highest number among non-Saudis. Five of those executions happened on Monday.
Two years ago, according to research by Amnesty International, just two Ethiopians were executed, but 35 were put to death in 2025.
It is not clear exactly why there has been an uptick, but it could be linked to more people leaving the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray, where a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray ended in late 2022, leaving devastation in its wake.
"It may also be linked to Saudi Arabia's expanding use of the death penalty for drug-related offences in recent years," Amnesty International researcher Dana Ahmed tells the BBC.
Habtom, who like most of the those the BBC spoke to is from Tigray, was found guilty of smuggling hashish, a type of cannabis. In Saudi Arabia, on the judge's discretion, a guilty verdict can result in a death sentence.
But rights groups - including Reprieve, Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International - have said that in these kinds of cases due process is rarely followed.
Defendants are not given access to a lawyer or the court papers - while translation, when it is offered, can be inadequate, Amnesty's Ahmed says.
Although there is the theoretical right to appeal, without a lawyer they cannot submit one "and then the sentence is automatically upheld", she says.
"There is a near-total lack of transparency throughout the entire judicial process, from sentencing to Supreme Court review and ratification by the King. People on death row and their families are left in the dark about their fate."
Habtom alleged that he was not given the chance to speak to a lawyer or defend himself. He also said he was forced to sign a document in Arabic, which said he agreed to the sentence, without understanding what he was putting his name to.
Other prisoners that the BBC spoke to had similar stories about the legal system.
HRW has also contacted people close to the cases and learned about "mass sentences, mass trials that lacked any kind of due process and people detained then just waiting with no idea when the sentence would happen", Nadia Hardman, the organisation's senior adviser on refugee and migrant rights, said.
The Saudi authorities did not respond to a BBC request for comment on allegations that the legal process was not fair, but every execution is accompanied by a statement issued through the official press agency. It outlines a clear process: an investigation, a court case, an appeal, a Supreme Court ruling and then a royal decree.
The sentence reflects the commitment to protect citizens "from the scourge of drugs" and the damage they can cause, the statement adds.
Habtom said that although he manged to keep in occasional contact with his family via the wall-mounted phone in his prison cell, he refused to tell them he was on death row: "I would rather they be told after I die than now."
He had dreamt of finishing high school, graduating from college and getting a job to support his parents - but the Tigray war put paid to that.
"My goal was destroyed, so I decided to emigrate," he said.
After surviving the dangerous journey to Saudi Arabia in 2021, Habtom found low-paid work as a goatherder, but his employers offered him and others a chance to earn more money.
They were asked to deliver a package but were stopped by police on the way and were found with the narcotic leaf known as khat - a natural stimulant that is widely used in the Horn of Africa.
The official Saudi statements all refer to hashish smuggling but those the BBC spoke to talked about khat.
"I did not know what we were carrying. But later I was told it was khat. I don't even know what khat is," Habtom said, admitting that he was tempted into the work by the sum of money on offer.
Habtom acknowledged he had "made a mistake without knowing it" and hoped that his sentence could be commuted to prison time.
Three of his fellow Ethiopian detainees were executed in April - another nine were killed in June. The April killings sparked an outcry from rights groups and some leading Ethiopian figures, including the influential head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
Patriarch Abune Mathias urged the government to negotiate with the Saudi authorities and called the inmates "voiceless children" living "under the shadow of death".
In its April report, HRW called on the Saudi authorities to immediately halt executions of Ethiopian migrants and ensure all cases were handled in line with international law. It also asked Ethiopia's foreign ministry to intervene urgently and provide consular support.
The safety of Ethiopians in general in Saudi Arabia was raised at a meeting in Addis Ababa in May between Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Al-Khuraiji.
This was followed in June by a visit to the prison by Ethiopia's Ambassador Tafa Tulu Dadi, though the prisoners told the BBC that they were not given enough time to explain their situation to him.
It also appeared to have limited impact as in the following week more Ethiopians were executed.
The African Union's human rights commission has also urged Ethiopia to safeguard the lives of Ethiopians facing execution in Saudi Arabia.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopian officials in Saudi Arabia and the government in Addis Ababa for comment but has not received a response.
Without referring to the death penalty specifically, Ethiopia's foreign ministry did release a statement on 13 July saying it was in regular contact with the Saudi authorities "pursuing appropriate remedies for Ethiopian citizens facing difficult circumstances".
It added that "to date" nearly 2,000 Ethiopians had "benefited from royal amnesties" - without mentioning the crimes or sentences.
As they await the outcome of diplomatic manoeuvres, the prisoners who spoke to the BBC said they were enduring hardships in overcrowded facilities.
Desta, located in another part of the prison, said there were 200 men in his cell crammed into an area designed for 90 people, with 45 bunk beds arranged around the walls.
During the day, the prisoners sat on the floor in stifling conditions squeezed up next to one another; when the temperature dropped at night, they covered themselves with rubbish bags in lieu of bed sheets, he said.
"The stress of facing execution, combined with the overcrowded conditions, exposes us to illness and anxiety," Desta said.

title: Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs
summary: President Donald Trump had blamed "sick" vandals, and a former Olympian had been charged, but prosecutors now say contractors caused the damage.
full_text:
Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs
- Published
US prosecutors have dropped charges against a former Olympian who had been accused of vandalising the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, writing in court documents that the damage is now believed to be "the result of flawed installation by the contractor".
President Donald Trump had previously blamed the damage on "sick, deranged" vandals.
But a document filed by prosecutors in Washington DC on Friday says new information "strongly suggests that a rushed and botched installation" job overseen by the US Department of Interior led to the damage.
David Hearn, a champion canoeist, had been facing a 10-year prison sentence if found guilty after his arrest last month.
In a statement, Hearn's lawyers accused the Trump administration of abuse of power, and said it "owes Mr Hearn an apology".
Hearn previously told the BBC that he "didn't destroy, rip, tear, peel, or remove any part" of the paint in the pool. Asked by the BBC on Friday if he is planning legal action over the government missteps that led to the charges and false public accusations, he declined to comment.
The document filed by US Attorney for Washington DC Jeanine Pirro blames contractors for rushing the paint installation process as part of Trump's efforts to beautify the city ahead of the country's 250th independence anniversary on 4 July.
Hearn was arrested after he said he reached down to touch the pool after a bike ride in the area.
He was not the only one. At least three others were charged with vandalism, court records show. Five more received citations from police, an administration official told CBS News, the BBC's US partner. They include one person who Trump claimed had used a blade "put a 250 foot long gash into the beautiful facade". It's unclear if all of the charges now have been dropped.
In the court filing on Friday, the Trump administration said new information from the Department of Interior (DOI) indicated "that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor" and "the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026".
"It was not until after these documents were produced that [prosecutors] first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI."
The BBC has contacted the contractor for comment.
Hearn's lawyers said in a statement to BBC News, that the case "should have never been brought".
"Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government's approach was ready, fire, aim."
The Reflecting Pool underwent a multi-million dollar resealing and painting project this spring.
The monument had long been beset by structural failures and leaks, and Trump championed the project as part of his bid to beautify the capital city.
But, despite the makeover, which cost an estimated $16m (£12m), the pool had continued to be plagued by algae, and pieces of the blue sealant peeled off within days after its application.
The project, whose original budget was less than $2m, was awarded to a contractor chosen by Trump himself, CBS reported, and was not open to bidding from other companies as is typical for government work.
The admission on Friday represents a stunning about face by Trump and his administration.
The US president at one point claimed the pool had been targeted by "sick, deranged" vandals, and was "given a 300 foot long gash" by a blade. Pirro accused Hearn of "a deliberate act to damage the Reflecting Pool."
Pirro submitted the court filing on Friday dropping the vandalism claim and blaming the contractor for the botched job and Department of Interior officials for failing to provide prosecutors with complete information about what caused the problems with the pool.
"DOI provided less than fulsome information at the outset of this case," the document said. "Had DOI been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment."
Crews have now drained the Reflecting Pool for the second time in three months. It remains empty.

title: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind
summary: Daniel Murphy went into psychosis after taking missold drugs which had been mixed with steroids.
full_text:
He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind
- Published
Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.
But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.
Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.
The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.
The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country.
His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.
Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.
Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.
Testosterone is a steroid hormone, which the body naturally produces. It drives physical development, builds muscle, and controls sex drive, primarily in males, but it also supports health in females.
There is a synthetic version which doctors can prescribe, but which can cause liver damage, serious psychiatric effects and heart and respiratory problems if taken without medical oversight. It can also cause infertility in men and increase the risk of testicular cancer.
The Paradigm Peptides case is the biggest to rock the industry, an unregulated market which has exploded into the mainstream over the past 18 months.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that our bodies produce and have long been used to treat medical conditions, including diabetes. More recently, they are being used in weight-loss drugs - GLP-1s.
Another type of drug sold by Paradigm Peptides was SARMs - Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators - which target specific tissues to increase muscle and bone mass.
Both these types of unregulated injectable drugs have become increasingly popular in the online wellness community - including among many young influencers.
Social media is inundated with people extolling the virtues of various substances - such as BPC-157, GHK-CU and TB 500 - all of which purport to help build muscle mass, help with tissue recovery, or improve skin health. They are not licensed, can only be sold for testing purposes and are not suitable for human consumption.
Three years ago, Murphy says he was in a good place. He was married to Laura, and they had built a "very stable, consistent, beautiful life" in the Smoky mountains in Knoxville, Tennessee.
Murphy had lost 130 pounds (59kg) and had "completed a major health transformation" through diet and exercise.
"I wasn't into gym culture - I wasn't a big gym bro or anything," he explains. "But after I had lost all that weight, I wanted to start building muscle and these supplements seemed like a safe way of doing that."
Murphy thought he was taking a daily dose of SARMs. Like peptides, they are not approved for human use and are seen as experimental drugs with a risk of serious liver damage, thrombosis and heart problems.
Murphy says he felt safe taking them because they were clearly labelled a "dietary supplement" and Paradigm claimed it had a contract with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on various blogs, but this was not true.
"Like other victims, I trusted that the products were safe," he says. "They presented everything as research backed with claims of 99% purity - it was all a lie."
Murphy started taking Paradigm's SARMs in January 2023. During the first few months, he says they seemed to be having a positive effect: he was able to do longer workouts and had more energy. Encouraged by fake research articles he had read on Paradigm Peptides's website, he then started taking other products too.
Insomnia and mania began to set in - and that triggered him, he says, to "burn down" everything he had built - his marriage, his friendships, and his business.
During the court proceedings, consultant psychiatrist and pharmacologist, Dr Erik Messamore, gave evidence to confirm that he believed Murphy had been suffering from a steroid-induced psychosis.
'UK consumers at risk'
As Murphy's life spun out of control, unknown to him, the FDA was already investigating Paradigm Peptides. It had been sending warning letters to the company since 2020 telling it to stop selling unapproved drugs. By September 2023, the FDA had seized SARMs products from Paradigm to carry out tests on them. It turned out, all the supplements had been mixed with testosterone.
But it would take another six months before the FDA closed the business down.
In the UK, Adam Taylor, professor of anatomy at Lancaster University, has been watching cases like this closely, as the scientific community continues to raise the alarm on this market which operates in a legal and regulatory middle zone. The products are not illegal to buy or own, but they are not approved for human use and so are not subject to the quality controls that govern pharmaceutical manufacturing.
"This might have happened in the US," Taylor says. "But consumers are at risk here in the UK, this is a global industry."
He says a case like this demonstrates the magnitude of the risk, when "people think they are taking one product but it's actually something completely different".
"So, they may also be getting additional side effects or different results that they can't explain."
Murphy's wife Laura says her husband changed overnight. He had gone from a "loving partner" to a man who believed that she was "plotting" to take over his successful consulting business.
"One minute he would be crying and asking what was wrong with him, the next he would talk about wanting to take over Los Angeles," she says. "We had no history of mental illness in our family, Dan was so calm and stable before this happened.
"We did not know what to do."
Life began to unravel. Murphy had an affair, was drinking copious amounts of alcohol, and felt his friends and family were out to get him - he even thought his mother-in-law wanted to murder him.
"I was in a full-blown psychosis - I believed that my loved ones were trying to hurt me and kill me," he recalls. "At this point, I've lost the plot. I'm not able to make any connection to the supplements, to anything that's happening."
Then in December 2024, Murphy ran out of his supply of Paradigm Peptides supplements. It was then, he says, he felt his condition began to improve.
Murphy and his family had no idea the FDA had been investigating the company, and it was not until February 2025 that he was told that the drugs he had been taking had been mixed with steroids.
"If only I had known, if the FDA had been more public, or even just put a notice on the Paradigm Peptides website. But instead, I'm taking this product and they know it's been cut with steroids," he says.
So far, he says he seems to have made a full recovery. He is one of 167 of the victims who have come forward and sought a total of $78,317 (£58,169) compensation for the damage caused. Others had suffered blood clots, heart issues, anxiety and depression, the Department of Justice confirmed.

title: I was working to survive and I wasn't paid
summary: Sonia Garcia Monuz is among ex-catering firm employees who claim they are owed unpaid wages.
full_text:
I was working to survive and I wasn't paid
- Published
What happens when your boss is also the HR department, the grievance handler and the person deciding whether you get paid?
"I just want my wages. It's my hard work. I just want what I'm owed."
Sonia Garcia Monuz is one of several workers trying to recover money she believes she is owed by a catering firm based in Berkshire.
Latest figures show early conciliation cases involving unpaid wages rose by about 17% between 2024 and 2025, according to Acas – the independent body that helps resolve workplace disputes.
Acas says nearly half of hospitality workers, 49%, experience problems at work.
Sonia began working as a full-time chef at Viking Catering Ltd in June 2024 and says the first six months were positive.
But after a series of disagreements with the owner, she handed in her notice and left in August 2025.
Sonia says she was never paid her final pay packet and is owed £2,300. She says she is not the only person affected.
"A lot of us are waiting for our wages to pay our bills," she says.
"Some people don't have savings. I was working to survive… I had to use my credit card in order to pay my rent and I had to ask for money from my family."
She has lodged a claim with Acas to try to recover the money, but says chasing her pay is "draining" and makes her feel "powerless".
Joan Fullbrook had hoped to enjoy her retirement, but instead says she is still chasing money she believes she is owed.
She worked for a different catering company owned by the same Hampshire-based businesswoman, Martha Lindeque.
"I worked hard every day in that kitchen and that was how I was repaid. It makes me sick to be treated this way," she says.
Employment tribunal records show Joan won a case against Chef2Table Ltd for "unauthorised deductions" from her wages after she left the business.
But she says the company never paid the £1,498 she was awarded.
"When you're working to live, these aren't small sums of money. It wasn't for luxuries, it was to survive. I was working to pay my bills," Joan adds.
Joan is now pursuing the money through the county courts.
George Weal was 21 when he started work at Chef2Table Ltd and says he is also owed money.
He left within months after discovering the company food van he drove to make deliveries was untaxed and uninsured.
This is something he says he had "no idea about" and that "could have led to me losing my licence".
George says he did not receive his final wages after leaving the business and felt "overwhelmed" when trying to recover the money.
Employment tribunal records show he was awarded £1,052 in January 2025 for unpaid wages, but he says the company never paid him.
"It was just really stressful. Especially for someone of my age," he says.
"I had the backing of parents in that financial sense, but some people don't, and could end up in a really bad situation with the loss of money."
Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline.
Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers on workplace rights and disputes.
"If someone is expecting their wages on a certain date and it doesn't arrive or it doesn't arrive in full, then if people haven't got savings, even a small amount of difference can be the difference between them paying their bills and not being able to pay them," says Chrissy.
She has this advice to anyone who believes they have not been paid the correct amount,
"Firstly, work out the amount you should have been paid. So check payslips, timesheets, contracts and the first step is to speak to the employers, as there may have been a genuine mistake."
If this does not work, she suggests putting a more formal grievance in writing, setting out any evidence, including timesheets, and then giving the employer a reasonable chance to respond.
Finally, she says if it is not resolved internally after a reasonable amount of time then the person should consider making a claim to an employment tribunal if they are owed outstanding wages.
"If someone gets an award at an employment tribunal then there are systems in place to help them enforce it if necessary," she says.
Martha Lindeque declined to provide a statement, but the BBC understands that her position is that she strongly denies the allegations made by her ex-staff.
