title: Police say 13 killed as small plane viewing Nazca Lines in Peru crashes
summary: Those killed included 11 passengers and two pilots flying over the famous archeological site, recognised by UNESCO.
full_text:
Police say 13 killed as small plane viewing Nazca Lines in Peru crashes
Those killed included 11 passengers and two pilots flying over the famous archeological site, recognised by UNESCO.
At least 13 people have been killed in a small plane that crashed in Peru, according to police.
The crash on Saturday came as the plane was carrying passengers, described by authorities as mostly tourists, to view the famous Nazca Lines, a series of archeological sites comprised of monumental geoglyphs carved into the soil.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3From first lady to president? Inside the rise of Peru’s Keiko Fujimori
- list 2 of 3At least 14 dead after minibus rolls off mountain road in Peru
- list 3 of 3Twin earthquakes strike Peru killing at least five
“We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died,” Police Major Jorge Andrade told reporters from the crash site in the country’s south.
Local media reports indicate that the crash site was quickly engulfed in flames, preventing any rescues. The plane reportedly departed from Pisco, in the department of Ica. Further details were not immediately available.
Peru is a major tourist destination, with visitors regularly travelling to visit the country’s historical sites, like the Incan ruins of Machu Picchu or the giant Indigenous stone walls of Cusco.
More than 4.1 million tourists visited the country of just under 35 million in 2025, according to Peru’s Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism.
The Nazca Lines are located in the desert near the country’s southern coastal regions, along the Andean mountain range.
They date back to between 500BC and 500AD, and have been designated as a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), in recognition of their value to global culture.
UNESCO describes the site as “among archaeology’s greatest enigmas because of their quantity, nature, size and continuity”.
“The geoglyphs depict living creatures, stylised plants and imaginary beings, as well as geometric figures several kilometres long,” according to UNESCO. “They are believed to have had ritual astronomical functions.”
Because of their enormous scale, the Nazca lines are often viewed from the air, where the drawings of animals like monkeys, hummingbirds and cats can be seen more clearly.
Saturday’s crash involved a plane from the fleet of the Peruvian sightseeing company Aerodiana, according to reports.

title: Fighting breaks out in western Tigray as Ethiopia and TPLF trade blame
summary: Clashes near Sheraro mark one of the most serious threats yet to the fragile 2022 Pretoria peace deal.
full_text:
Fighting breaks out in western Tigray as Ethiopia and TPLF trade blame
Clashes near Sheraro mark one of the most serious threats yet to the fragile 2022 Pretoria peace deal.
Fighting has broken out in western Tigray, in one of the most serious breaches yet of the three-year-old peace deal between Ethiopia’s federal government and fighters in the northern region.
Tigray’s regional government said in a statement from Mekelle, the Tigrayan capital, that federal forces opened the assault at dawn on Saturday, advancing from the direction of Sheraro, near the Sudanese border.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US government mislabels countries on map of Africa at global conference
- list 2 of 3Who is driving diplomacy in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and why?
- list 3 of 3Why is Uganda experiencing a food crisis?
Abraham Belay, a government minister who led Tigray’s transitional government during the war, confirmed the clashes but accused Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) chairman Debretsion Gebremichael’s forces of starting them.
“Enough war! Let us resolve our differences through dialogue,” he said in a post on Facebook.
The fighting follows months of deteriorating relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF, the party that ruled Ethiopia for nearly three decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018.
Both sides have accused each other of failing to implement the provisions of the 2022 peace agreement.
Tigrayan authorities said Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party has waged a long blockade and drone campaign against the region, adding that this had now escalated into full-scale war.
The regional government urged Tigrayan forces, civil society and religious institutions to prepare for a struggle it called one of national survival, using the slogan “No to National Destruction”.
Getachew Reda, a former TPLF spokesman who now advises Abiy, separately urged the Tigray Defence Forces commanders to abandon Debretsion, accusing him of relying on Eritrea and Amhara’s Fano militia to force his way back to power.
Reda and Redwan Hussein, Ethiopia’s intelligence chief, who signed the Pretoria deal for TPLF and the federal government respectively in 2022, co-wrote an Al Jazeera op-ed in June warning that war was imminent.
Kjetil Tronvoll, an Ethiopia specialist at Oslo New University College, told Al Jazeera that the fighting marked the “most serious incident” since the 2022 peace deal. The deal, Tronvoll added, halted the war between the two parties but left “the core reasons of conflict between Mekelle and Addis” unresolved.
In the days running up to the armed clashes, Ethiopian state media ran a campaign accusing Debretsion by name of rallying Tigrayans toward war.
The fighting caps months of escalating confrontation since the Pretoria Agreement of November 2022, which ended a war that began two years earlier and killed hundreds of thousands, but left unresolved deeper disputes over disarmament and the TPLF’s legal status.
In June, the United States imposed visa restrictions on what it said were TPLF “hardliners” accused of blocking peace. The TPLF described it as being based on an “incomplete and imbalanced” picture of the standoff.
By mid-July, TPLF had declared the Pretoria agreement “effectively dead”, even as US Ambassador Ervin Massinga travelled to Mekelle to try to preserve the deal.
Faisal Roble, a regional analyst, told Al Jazeera that the beginning of the fighting was a sign that efforts to resolve the dispute between the parties by the US had not succeeded.
“Without a powerful international intervention,” he said, “we could be heading to a much larger war.”

title: From Mao to now: why China’s Communist Party is  intent on control over the military
summary:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just one year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the third part of a series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng examine how Beijing leans on Mao-era doctrines and anti-corruption drives to guarantee absolute party control over the armed forces.
In December 1929, then Communist revolutionary Mao Zedong led a pivotal meeting in...
full_text:
From Mao to now: why China’s Communist Party is intent on control over the military
Beijing’s anti-corruption clean-up of the military reflects a historic commitment to party control, ensuring the armed forces strictly serve party goals
In December 1929, then Communist revolutionary Mao Zedong led a pivotal meeting in Gutian, Fujian province.
The next two decades witnessed some of the defining moments leading up to the Communist victory of 1949, including the Long March, the consolidation of Mao’s leadership and the renaming of the armed forces as the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
In 1938, as the party faced a turning point following the departure of co-founder and Mao’s revolutionary rival Zhang Guotao, Mao wrote: “Our principle is that the party commands the gun, and the gun must never be allowed to command the party.”
Nearly a century on, those principles still serve as the political bedrock of the party’s control over the military.

title: A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino?
summary: The pressure is building on Gianni Infantino. Can he survive as Fifa president?
full_text:
A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino?
- Published
A week is a long time in politics. Football politics.
On Tuesday morning, Gianni Infantino was in an impregnable position as Fifa president, the most powerful job in football.
Now, after trying to sells stakes in Fifa competitions to private investments firms - apparently without the knowledge of anyone else - Infantino's position appears to be under threat.
Uefa - Infantino's fiercest critic - dealt its trump card on Thursday by threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.
Now European football's governing body senses the opportunity to remove Infantino - and this is likely to be the best chance it will ever get.
But they're far from the only unhappy federation.
Concacaf, the confederation Infantino worked so closely with to organise the 2026 World Cup, has called for a "full review" into the leadership of Fifa in light of Infantino's plan.
Even more damaging, loyal countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) shunned him too.
Then he was abandoned by two of his closest allies - first senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro and then chief operating officer Kevin Lamour.
After Infantino backtracked in the early hours of Saturday morning, Uefa delivered another devastating blow by issuing a strong statement saying it had lost confidence in him.
The battles lines have been drawn. What could happen next?
- Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Four reasons why Fifa's World Cup plan never stacked up 
  - Published11 hours ago
- Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes? 
  - Published13 hours ago
How could Infantino be ousted?
The quickest route for Infantino's exit would be for the Swiss to resign, like his predecessor Sepp Blatter did in 2015.
But Infantino still retains support and he could try to hold out until March, when he is up for re-election for a fourth and final term as president.
What other avenues are open?
The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.
Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.
Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.
BBC Sport understands there are some doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved.
If they do get to 19, the meeting must take place within two weeks and the Fifa Council could call on Infantino to tender his resignation. But he could simply refuse to do so.
It would, however, add further pressure.
The next step would be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".
So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it so wishes.
That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.
In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence.
Uefa has 55, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.
Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan.
So could Uefa get to 106? In total, 136 countries officially rejected the investment plan, but voting to reject an idea is not the same as voting to kick Infantino out.
Of the 136, Qatar have already publicly backed him and Mexico have distanced themselves from the joint Concacaf statement.
Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election in March.
Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.
- The five dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football 
  - Published11 hours ago
Who could potentially replace Infantino?
If Uefa and Infantino's biggest critics have to go down the election route, they will need to find a unifying leader.
As Uefa has been so strong in its opposition to Infantino, a European candidate might struggle to get global support. After all, it might seem like it is trying to take over Fifa itself.
So there must be a candidate who can attract the support of those countries in Concacaf, Africa and Asia who could have been loyal to Infantino but could be persuaded to switch their votes.
The most likely candidate appears to be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani.
Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to and delivery of the 2026 World Cup. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.
Another option would be Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president.
Initially elected in 2013, he was re-elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.
Sheikh Salman signed off the confederation's brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.
Less likely appears to be Paris St-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari who is also the chair of European Football Clubs.
Al-Khelaifi helped bring European football back together after another seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League.
In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. Qatar's support for Infantino could be an issue, too.
How likely is it that Infantino is ousted?
In any other business, Infantino would be unlikely to continue in his role.
But football, of course, is not a normal business.
Remember Sepp Blatter, who resigned in 2015 when he had no option left amid a corruption scandal. He had even been re-elected the week before.
So will Infantino try to fight on?
In his statement on Saturday, he said his intent "was to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks".
For Infantino, contrition could make this all float away.
Maybe it is working. Following on from Qatar, 2030 co-hosts Morocco backed him on Saturday evening. Then Egypt praised Infantino for cancelling his masterplan.
Infantino may be thinking that if he can, day by day, get more member associations on board, the prospect of a vote of no confidence is less likely to be successful.
After all, his support base has been so strong for so long you can understand why he might have such confidence.
As a vote of no confidence is three months away, he has the chance to repair at least some of the damage.
It is a race to 106 - and the more time elapses, the more chance Infantino can persuade his former allies this was just an aberration.
For Uefa, the question is whether it can create a situation whereby Infantino is left with no option but to resign.
For that to happen, the criticism from federations across the world must continue.
But if there is one thing that could damage Infantino further, it would be for major sponsors to distance themselves from the organisation.
During the 2015 Fifa scandal, Sony, Emirates, Castrol, Continental Tyres and Johnson & Johnson were among the companies to discontinue their huge sponsorship deals.
There is no sign of this just yet but this is a saga with the potential to rumble on.

title: Young guns for hire - the teenage hitmen recruited to kill across Europe
summary: The Foxtrot Network is thought to be responsible for about 35 murders in Europe, and uses violence-as-a-service tactics.
full_text:
Young guns for hire - the teenage hitmen recruited to kill across Europe
- Published
In a Stockholm suburb a man dressed in black appeared out of the winter night. Carrying a handgun, he approached 20-year-old Murad Abdelkader, a student on his way back from a shift at McDonald's.
The gunman opened fire, shooting again and again as he approached his target. He fired the last shot into his victim's head as he lay helpless on the ground.
The killer was 18-year-old Atilla Azimov. On that February night last year, he had killed the wrong man.
He had done it for money - hired by the Foxtrot Network, an organised crime group with links to the Iranian regime which has become notorious for its violence-as-a-service (VaaS) tactics.
Since 2022, the Foxtrot Network is thought to have been responsible for about 35 murders as well as a number of attacks and attempted attacks on Israeli targets in Europe including two involving explosives and hand grenades.
The gang recruits teenagers to carry out the attacks for cash, but it almost never has to pay out as they often get caught.
Like Johannes Natland, a Norwegian teenager who was convicted of conspiracy to murder by a jury at the Old Bailey in London on Wednesday for a planned killing in West Yorkshire.
According to Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, the Europol group set up to tackle the problem, the teenage hitmen are recruited on social media, and are given their instructions in a "gamified" way, imitating how computer games work.
Andy Kraag, the head of Europol's European Serious and Organised Crime Centre, calls it the "calculated outsourcing of murder" to vulnerable young people.
OTF GRIMM currently involves 11 countries affected by the VaaS phenomenon - Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.
The leader of the Foxtrot Network, Rawa Majid, has fled Sweden and his later operating base in Turkey, and is now based in the Iranian capital Tehran. Police believe some of the VaaS attacks have been carried out for the Iranian regime, including a hand grenade attack on the Israeli embassy in Copenhagen, though other attacks are part of Foxtrot's drugs turf wars.
Diamant Salihu, an investigative journalist for the Swedish broadcaster SVT, has been researching Foxtrot and its Iranian links for three years.
"The regime is ordering the leader of the Foxtrot Network to instigate his network to commit attacks against the Iranian regime's enemies," he said.
"It can be dissidents, journalists that are in the opposition against the regime, and it can also be Israeli targets."
The links to the Iranian regime started after October 2023 when Majid fled to Tehran, Salihu said.
"He had to make a deal to be able to live freely in Iran, under condition that he and his network work for the regime."
The Foxtrot Network and Majid were sanctioned by the UK government, external in April 2025.
That was the month after the arrest of Natland, who was 18 at the time. He had flown in to carry out a hit on behalf of Foxtrot somewhere near Huddersfield.
The Natland case illustrates how the VaaS system works.
Natland is the son of two journalists in Stavanger and had a comfortable upbringing, but he drifted into drugs and developed psychosis, ending up spending time in rehab and a short period in a children's home. There he met another teenager who used the online handle UnknownHustler.
It was UnknownHustler who first sent Natland the online request for someone to carry out a hit in the UK - "Killing in England 270k" (270,000 Norwegian kroner is about £21,000). It had come from another teenager with the handle Generalen. Generalen - who was 16 at the time and had spent the last three years living in a children's home - subsequently recruited Natland for the hit.
Natland was then passed on to a Foxtrot member with the online username Agent 47, which is borrowed from the Hitman game franchise. Swedish police have accused Ali Shehad Ahmed, who is close to the Foxtrot leader Majid, of being Agent 47.
Agent 47 booked Natland's one way ticket to Manchester Airport, and helped him through the process of getting an emergency passport. Using the messaging app Signal, he guided Natland at every stage of his journey before handing him on to a logistics man with the username "1".
Treating Natland a bit like a character in a computer game, "1" sent him a map and videos showing him where to find the guns hidden in woodland in Huddersfield, and then another video showing him how to access a stash of cash hidden in the undergrowth near a foot tunnel.
Once Natland was installed in his Huddersfield hotel with the weapons, Agent 47 messaged him again: "We have much to do tomorrow."
Natland was arrested the next morning. He had not yet been told who he was to kill, and counterterrorism detectives are still trying to work out whether it was to be a criminal hit or a political one carried out for Iran.
- Sweden ditches plan to imprison 13-year-old serious offenders 
  - Published11 June
The teenager who recruited Natland - Generalen - was prolific. As well as hiring Natland as a hitman he had also recruited at least two people who carried out murders in Sweden. They were Azimov, who is serving a life sentence for killing the wrong man, and a 17-year-old who shot dead Ahmed Zamzam in Lund, south Sweden, three and a half weeks earlier.
Neither of the killers got paid, because they were both caught. Salihu said this was part of how Foxtrot worked.
"They don't care at all if the teenagers get caught. Because when they get caught, they cannot ask for money that they have been offered, and we see no examples of money being paid to these young killers," he said.
"It has been a deliberate policy to recruit younger and younger teenagers because they don't think about the consequences of getting caught, and they are more willing to take the risks."
Generalen was eventually stopped because he was trying to arrange the murder of the 14-year-old son of a Norwegian police officer. He recruited a 15-year-old and a 17-year-old to carry out the knife attack, but the 15-year-old told the police. When Generalen was arrested detectives found details of the Huddersfield murder plot on his phone that led to British police arresting Natland just in time.
Generalen was convicted in May and is serving a 14-year-prison sentence.
OTF GRIMM has had some successes in the 15 months since it was set up. Police have made more than 280 arrests including a few key suspects.
One of the most important arrests was that of Ahmed, who is thought to be Agent 47.
He was detained in the Kurdish city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq, and is currently subject to an extradition request to Sweden.
The Swedish deputy national police commissioner Stefan Hector said they were "constantly expanding our co-operation with other countries" and showing organised criminals "they cannot feel safe anywhere in the world".
In May, Mohamed "Moewgli" Mohdhi, a former rapper described by Swedish police as a "central actor" in Foxtrot, was arrested in Tunisia.
But Majid himself remains out of reach in Iran.
"He's still active," Salihu said. "And as long as this network is active we will still continue, I fear, to see attacks on the enemies of the Iranian regime."
It is not yet clear the extent to which the arrests have degraded Foxtrot's ability to operate, but other groups - including Foxtrot's rivals the Dalen Network - have already adopted the VaaS method of recruiting vulnerable teenagers for murders, so the danger is still very present.
It spread quickly from Sweden across Scandinavia and northern Europe and, as the Natland case shows, reached the UK last year.

title: I had a vasectomy in my 20s after the trauma of my sons' births
summary: As the number of young men having vasectomies rises, BBC News spoke to two about why they chose to have the snip.
full_text:
I had a vasectomy in my 20s after the trauma of my sons' births
- Published
Alex West was left harrowed by the difficult labour his wife endured for their first child. When it came to their second, he hoped for a much smoother arrival.
The birth did go better for his wife - but not for him.
"I had a panic attack and broke down. I hadn't been able to - I didn't have the ability to - process that," Alex says.
Unresolved trauma from his wife's first labour and his subsequent postnatal depression meant Alex didn't want to continue with the couple's plan to have four children.
- Vasectomies even safer than reported, doctors say 
  - Published12 March 2023
He remembers the months after the births of his two sons as "grey" - life was devoid of colour and filled with people telling him that being a father must be a fantastic experience.
"I didn't feel this love and connection that everybody says I should have," Alex says.
Not wanting to repeat the experience, he and his wife agreed to stop at two kids. Given he was the driving force behind the decision, he felt it was "wrong to put the onus on my wife" to take a contraceptive.
So like thousands more men in England have done in recent years, Alex chose to have a vasectomy.
The procedure involves the cutting and then clamping or sealing of the vas deferens, a tube on each testicle that carries sperm to the urethra. It's colloquially known as the snip.
Some 26,385 vasectomies were performed at hospitals and clinics during 2024-25, according to data compiled by NHS England. This was 16% more than in 2023-24.
Men aged 35-39 had more procedures than any other age group, about 8,400 in 2024-25.
There had also been a slight rise on the previous year in younger men choosing to have the snip - about 950 vasectomies were performed on men aged under 30 in England during 2024-25.
Fears about pregnancy
Alex, a mortgage broker, decided in his late 20s to have the procedure but his NHS doctor urged him to wait until he turned 30 in case he changed his mind.
When the appointment came in May 2024, he and his wife took the train from their Kent home to the London clinic.
The procedure was quick and painless says Alex, now 33. "I put my headphones on and I listened to about three songs before they said it was all done.
"Ridiculous - crazy quick."
Sam Knight, who's from the US, says he knew he didn't want to have children.
"I was putting myself in situations where kids could be a potential option and that really started to, kind of, freak me out," Sam says.
When his then-partner became pregnant, she chose to have an abortion and Sam, aged 22 at the time, felt a change was needed.
"[I had] a realisation of this thing that I've put somebody through and I just didn't want that to ever happen again."
He contacted a urology clinic in New York and, like Alex, had to explain to clinicians why he wanted a vasectomy. Sam was advised the procedure should be treated as permanent, as it can only be reversed in some circumstances.
Strict criteria for reversals
Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?
"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."
His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.
The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.
Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".
But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them.
"We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just to… make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision."
She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one.
The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.
Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.
"I've devoted my life to this and, to me, parenting is something you also devote your life to," Sam says. "I just don't have the mental space or the time to do that, or even the desire to."
Sam, now 25, says he envies those who do want to become parents because the experience "clearly has" beauty and love in it. But adds, "I find that in music and art and these things that I do."
The procedure in 2024 and the aftercare cost Sam, who was still on his family's health insurance policy, about $1,200 (£849) in total.
He's among fewer than 1% of men in the US aged 18-29 who have ever had a vasectomy, according to the National Survey of Family Growth, which analysed the responses of about 4,000 men in 2022-23.
Men in their mid to late 40s were most likely to have had one -15% said they had.
Sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent
Sam experienced one bout of excruciating pain a week after the procedure, a known but uncommon side effect of vasectomies according to Dr Salkeld, but that subsided after a few hours.
He doesn't think this should put other men off having a vasectomy. "Overall, it is worth the money and it is worth the pain," he says.
Another man told us the sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent - particularly how his children might turn out - drove him to have a vasectomy aged 27.
Back in Kent, the decision to get the snip felt like the fairest and most effective form of contraception available to Alex and his wife.
It was something they considered carefully over several months, knowing they no longer wanted more children.
"I absolutely adore my children," Alex says, particularly now they are old enough to play football with.
"If I had added more to the team, it wouldn't have been the right thing for me."

title: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
summary: For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade or more.
full_text:
Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
- Published
For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade.
The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity.
His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach.
His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap".
"I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC.
"Then all these people got in touch."
"I was like 'oh wow, of course, the whole world is in the States'," Kieran says. "It's a microcosm."
He says a message from a Native American man who had red hair instantly aroused his curiosity.
"I found it very interesting and it made me think, 'where on earth did it come from?'"
The cover of his latest book - Gingers of America, external - features Joshua Elliot from the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma.
He told Kieran that some of his mother's relatives were German and on his dad's side there were people from England and Sweden, so that could explain where his ginger hair comes from.
"My mom's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribe and traditions and I've grown up around it," he said.
Joshua knows he does not fit people's expectations of what a Native American should look like, but he said: "Our chief's wife told me it's about your involvement in your community and your tribe, the people around you and what you put back into it.
"Which I really took to heart."
Kieran spoke to a lot of Native Americans on his visits and most knew of a European ancestry which could explain their red hair.
"The thing that surprised me was how early on there were these Scots and Irish marrying Native Americans," he said.
Lottie Wahkinney, a Comanche girl from Oklahoma, has Scottish grandparents, from Galashiels.
Her father Jared told Kieran his dad was Comanche but his mum was born and raised in Scotland.
"That's why my Lottie has a good mix of everything going on," Jared said.
"My Scottish grandparents would come over every summer.
"On my first visit to Scotland when I was 22, folks were like, 'Where are your moccasins? Where's your headdress?'.
"I explained 'I wear Nikes'."
While most Native Americans could explain where the ginger gene might have come from, there was one exception - a Cherokee girl called Lakia - whose family knew of no European ancestry.
"It is a totally different colour of red," Kieran said.
"It's deep ruby. That really intrigued me."
In the book, Lakia says that all her family, on both sides, have jet-black straight hair but hers turned red during her childhood.
"Everyone thought, since I was about eight, that I dyed my hair," she said.
"And still now everyone's like, 'what hair colour is that?'."
After meeting Native Americans, Kieran knew there was something in the US he could explore.
Over the next few years, he made seven lengthy trips, often linked to his full-time profession as an environmental photographer.
One state he found surprising was Alabama, a place many in the UK associate with racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights as well as its pioneering space exploration programmes.
"I knew it for racism and Nasa," Kieran said.
"In my head it was stuck in the 60s but Birmingham is an incredibly vibrant city.
"I met a lot of black Americans who had often married someone who is white."
Rachel Releford told Kieran that when she goes out with her daughter Liliana people think she is the nanny or the babysitter.
"I'm like, 'nope, she's mine'," Rachel said.
"I think you still get some people who grew up with the mindset that things need to be segregated.
"Some of my grandparents' friends were a little hesitant when they found out I was dating my husband. They said: 'You're really going to let her date someone of a different race?'
"But my grandparents were like, 'Go for it. He's a cool guy, he's a sweet one.' I love him for who he is. He's a great human being."
Also in Alabama, he met Henry Davis and his young son Henry Davis II.
The older man no longer has any red hair but he says he looked just like his son when he was the same age.
"We're not really sure where it comes from," Henry senior said.
"My dad is turning grey now. He'll get some red in his beard, and then it kind of goes grey.
"So I guess it's from his side."
As someone who grew up with red hair himself, Kieran says he is well aware that ginger can be used as an insult.
However, he says: "I use the word for its descriptive power because red is the colour of fire engines and blood whereas ginger has a golden tone to it.
"You can use it in a kind way."
He says the book uses ginger hair as "a golden thread" that weaves together America's diverse and difficult history in a way which shows a connection between people.
"That's my big idea," Kieran says.
"We are all made of the same stuff and with the ginger hair it shows."
According to Kieran no-one exemplifies this better than a young lad named Cali whom he met in Alabama.
"His background is everything - European, African-American, Hispanic and indigenous as well," he says.
"His gran is white but was she unable to get married to a black guy in Alabama - even after the courts had made it legal.
"She moved to Georgia and had a family there. It's an incredibly diverse family."
In Scotland, it is thought as many as 13% of the population - about 700,000 people - are natural redheads, a higher percentage than anywhere else in the world.
Globally, less than 2% of the population are thought to have red hair but Kieran's research lead him to believe the US figure is higher than that.
"We landed on about 4% for the genetic prevalence," he says.
"If all the gingers in America were gathered in one place, Gingertown would be about 14 million people.
"It's a big city. You would see it from space it would be so bright."
Kieran says the big difference between America and other places is that they tend to have really thought about where they come from.
"Everyone has self-consciously moved from somewhere," he says.
"And that includes the Native Americans, who have been moved from other parts of America.
"That's what makes it interesting."
He says his book is a road trip through the US trying to find out about the country through this unique trait.
For Kieran, the recent men's football World Cup got people excited about the US again in a way they haven't been over the past few years because of political divisions.
He says he was pleased to see people visiting the US and saying "it is not what I expected".
"There's such a lot of amazing people and communities there," he says.
"People you might connect with and agree with on a lot of things.
"I'm quite heartened that the football has revealed that.
"I feel quite patriotic for America now."

title: Spider-Man fans hail Brand New Day as Holland's best yet
summary: Spider-Man fans are full of praise for Tom Holland's latest web-slinging performance.
full_text:
Spider-Man fans hail Brand New Day as Holland's best yet
- Published
Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.
Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.
The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.
Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.
There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.
'Still Marvel's ace in the pack'
The reviews from critics have been largely positive.
Many critics have welcomed the film-makers' decision to scale back from the multiverse seen in No Way Home, in favour of a more personal, character-centred story.
The Telegraph's Robbie Collin called it, external "the best Spider-Man film since the Tobey Maguire era", and praised the relationship between Holland and Zendaya, who create a "real yearning and perplexity" that we have not seen previously in the dynamic between their characters.
In his review for The Wrap, William Bibbiani, external described it as the strongest entry in Holland's Spider-Man series, applauding its emotional focus and character-driven storytelling, and praising its "wonderful, propulsive quality".
Meanwhile, Empire's John Nugent awarded the film four stars, external, declaring the web-slinging hero is "still Marvel's ace in the pack", and in its five-star review The Standard said the film had "verve, intelligence and above all, heart".
However, others have been more reserved.
The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw declared, external that Zendaya "saves this film" from "silliness and the generic déjà vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it".
This opinion was supported by David Rooney in the Hollywood Reporter, external, who wrote that the film "chugs along satisfyingly even with the occasional patch of sluggishness and the usual overly convoluted plot contortions".
He adds: "As much as the movie revels in the thrill of Spidey swinging between skyscrapers with erratic command of his shooters, the more intimate scenes with MJ and Ned are what supplies the emotional charge."
Danny Leigh of the Financial Times awarded the film three stars, external, praising the chemistry between Holland and Zendaya but criticising the film's insistence on falling back on CGI-heavy action sequences.
But that is just what the critics say. What do audiences think?
Fresh from a screening of the film, Sam said "I have been a Spider-Man fan since I was six years old, but it's only in the last decade I have really got into it, all because of these films".
He called Brand New Day his favourite film of Holland's tenure, praising him for the "most mature performance" as the character to date.
Kimberly agreed, but said while Holland does a "fantastic job" she still has a soft spot for "the OG" Tobey Maguire.
Maguire played the role in three movies directed by Sam Raimi from 2002 to 2007.
Spidey fan Joe praised Holland's handling of the famous character over the years, saying his version of Spider-Man has "shown his progression" over the years.
"Half his life he has been doing this character. He's handled it very well."
Asked how he felt about Holland one day leaving the franchise, he said: "I hope not! I think we still have a lot more to see from him."
Clutching her Spider-Man popcorn bucket, Danika was more open to the idea of a passing of the baton, saying Zendaya and Holland have "had a good run" so she would not be disappointed "as long as they end the characters in a good way."
She said Zendaya's acting in particular was "amazing," and labelled Brand New Day as "the most comic accurate Spider-Man movie".
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is poised to become one of Marvel's most successful movies at the box office, and Sony will be hoping to emulate the returns of Holland's previous outing, Spider-Man: No Way Home.
Released in 2021, the film benefited massively from the return of previous Spider-Man actors Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield and went on to gross $1.9 bn (£1.4bn) worldwide., external
So, what next for the franchise's stars?
Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.
Ten years and multiple other blockbusters later, there is an ever-growing speculation that their futures now lie away from the MCU.
Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, external with Josh Horowitz, Holland hinted that a new chapter was on the horizon, albeit not clarifying when.
"It's going to change, for sure", he said.
"There is a whole plan that we have been working on since, I would say, Spider-Man No Way Home.
"I have a really clear vision to the passing on of the baton, and I think it is really exciting."
As for Zendaya, she has hinted previously that she is planning on taking a career break at the end of 2026, after a busy schedule that included the promotion of her films The Drama, The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Dune: Part Three.
Earlier this year Zendaya told Elle, external that "I think that after this, I'm going to have to take a little bit of a break".
She backed this notion up when asked about her future plans, external by Entertainment Tonight at the NYC premiere of The Odyssey, replying, "Oh, girl, nothing. Just mind my business!".

title: Does Love Island UK need to pull the US version for a chat?
summary: Fans, commentators and an ex-Islander reflect on what the dating series could do to draw in more viewers again.
full_text:
Love Island has a problem, say fans - 'there hasn't been much love'
- Published
What's your dream Love Island series on paper?
Some watch for the heartwarming romances, like Molly-Mae Hague and Tommy Fury falling for each other back in 2019, while others prefer intense dramas - we see you 2022 winners Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu and Davide Sanclimenti.
Others tune in for exciting challenges like Snog, Marry, Pie or the ones which literally send heart rates soaring.
For most, it's a mix of all of the above, and it's a balance TV producers have been trying to strike for years with the original UK series, as well as a host of spin-offs and international editions.
It's no secret that Love Island UK linear viewing figures have dropped from their 2019 heyday, with streaming and social media becoming more of a focus.
Across the pond the US edition has been reaching new heights, with the latest eighth series ranked as the number one reality show for five weeks in the States across all streaming platforms, according to its streamer Peacock. , external
It also had an injection of star power as US celebrity fans, including Lizzo, Demi Lovato and Kesha, sent messages of support to the finalists, while rapper Megan Thee Stallion has become a regular guest.
BBC Newsbeat has been speaking to fans, commentators and an ex-Islander to see what they feel the UK edition could learn from the US version to regain its spark.
The 13th series of the UK show ended on Monday, with Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi crowned the winners.
The final drew in an average audience of 1.1m viewers across all devices, including streaming, according to its broadcaster ITV, but this was a notable drop from last year's, which had an overnight audience of 1.3m.
By comparison, series five in 2019 broke the show's viewing records with 6m tuning in to an episode post Casa Amor, and that year's final had the highest average audience to date.
However, ITV say this 2019 figure was a consolidated number reached once it "had received all the data post final" and said it do not yet have an "equitable" figure for Series 13.
According to the network, more than 60% of its audience now engage with the show through streaming and the latest series, as well as its companion shows Aftersun and The Debrief, have had more than 180 million streams on ITVX.
Content creator Sarel, known for her Love Island debriefs to her 1.2m followers on TikTok, feels the biggest issue with the most recent UK series is "there hasn't been much love" between the couples, so she wasn't rooting for anyone at the end.
And while she knows people watch it for the drama and conversations it sparks, she thinks those are just "added extras" and the romances should be at the centre of the show.
"I want somebody to fall in love. I love stories where we get the butterfly moments," she says.
"Where you had your Indiyah [Polack] and your Dami [Hope] when they ran to each other, or you had couples like Molly-Mae and Tommy."
She thinks that's an aspect which the US version has been getting right, as it feels like "everyone who is in there actually fancies one another" and there is "no box" they have to fit into.
Someone from the UK who chose to go on the US version is Aaron Evans, but this wasn't his first reality series as he was one of three winners on the first series of The Traitors UK.
He feels the US edition's success is helped by having "fresh eyes" on the format and the show having "so much social media presence", which makes it "highly engaging".
Stats given to Newsbeat by TikTok - which called Love Island "one of the most influential entertainment franchises" on the app - suggest he's not wrong.
During the latest series, the hashtag #LoveIsland was mentioned in 123,000 posts in the UK, with #LoveIslandUK featuring in 88,000.
While in the US, #LoveIsland appeared in 1.09m posts and #LoveIslandUSA was tagged in 502,000 posts.
That said, the US population is nearly five times the size of the UK's.
US entertainment journalist Carly Thomas says executive producers have told her they look for ways to "bring in the US audience", be that through social media, challenges and the islanders they choose.
"I think for the US audience, we love to just relate and connect with people," Thomas, who works for The Hollywood Reporter, says.
She also feels the US edition wants to "push the limits" of the islanders with intense challenges and viewers "love to see how far they'll go", including rapper Megan Thee Stallion hosting one which saw them sit on cakes and throw them at each other.
Love Island USA has not been all smooth sailing, though.
Contestants in last year's series faced relentless online bullying which forced the show to broadcast a statement saying it does not tolerate "cyberbullying, harassment or hate". The show insists it takes duty of care seriously.
The US version runs for six weeks once a year, while the UK summer edition typically airs across eight weeks.
There is also now an additional series in the UK throughout the year, with a winter edition airing in 2020 and 2023, which has now been succeeded by All Stars.
The finale of the third All Stars version, which sees ex-islanders return to the villa, attracted about 910,000 viewers earlier this year.
During the most recent UK series, producers tried to get hearts racing, and TikTok numbers up, by introducing some new twists.
A few islanders were summoned for a sleepover at a different villa before Casa Amor, and for the first time, only three couples were in the final after two pairs got dramatically dumped.
Some fans have appreciated the changes, while others, like Sarel, feel they didn't land.
Love Island superfan Dami Amoo, who has watched every episode of the UK, US and All Star editions, says the UK series is starting to feel "overproduced".
"I do think it's been on a steady decline because they're trying to give us what we want, but then they're overdoing it and then they're taking away the classic [elements]."
She thinks this may have been due to budget constraints, but missed the islanders going on exciting dates and taking part in "fun activities or games" where you see their personalities more.
Amoo, 28, also thinks you can really see the impact of investment in the US version, which was aired almost simultaneously with the latest UK edition.
"They've invested so much into the props, the games and all of these brands are part of the actual production," she says.
"Whereas the UK version, it seems like they're just on an island somewhere just doing it on their own.
"You don't get a lot of hype, we don't get British celebrities contributing to the discussions."
'Everything's just very American'
The US edition has been able to bring in revenue by becoming a major space for advertising, external, with numerous content partners and more than 1,000 media partners, according to Peacock.
Evans isn't surprised by the US version capitalising on brand partnerships, saying "everything's bigger, everything's brighter, everything's just very American".
So as the sun sets on another run of Love Island series, what could UK producers do ahead of the next launch?
Superfan Dami thinks "they should really get some real fans in the production room".
"The people that do the debriefs online, people who engage on Twitter, they should get us in a room and we tell them what we really, really want."
An ITV spokesperson told Newsbeat "reaction of the fans is at the heart of the show as seen in public votes and including opinions as part of the challenges."
They added Love Island UK "continues to wield huge cultural relevance, both in the UK and in the USA" and to date it has had "over 2bn streams on ITVX and remains the biggest 16-34 show in commercial television".
Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Srosh Khan and Jack Gray.

title: The Sopranos star Vincent Pastore dies aged 80
summary: Pastore, who played Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero in the hit US show, was found at his home in New York City, US media report.
full_text:
The Sopranos star Vincent Pastore dies aged 80
- Published
US actor Vincent Pastore, who played Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero in the hit show The Sopranos, has died aged 80, according to several US outlets.
Pastore was found at his home in the Bronx, New York City and there was no indication of criminality, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
In The Sopranos, Pastore played Tony Soprano's best friend who ultimately became an informant for the FBI. His character's death in series two was one of the show's most memorable storylines.
Robert Attermann, Pastore's manager, told CBS News: "To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable 'Big Pussy,' but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more."
"He loved being an actor. He was passionate about his craft and was always encouraging, respectful, and generous with young actors, taking the time to offer guidance and support whenever he could," Attermann said.
He continued: "For me, losing Vinny is deeply personal. Over more than three decades, I had the honor of watching not only his remarkable career but also the incredible person he was. I will miss his friendship, his loyalty, his humor, and his heart."
Pastore was born in the Bronx in 1946. He enlisted in the US Navy during the Vietnam War before embarking on a career in acting.
His early credits included roles in movies such as Goodfellas and Carlito's Way.
Later TV appearances included Law & Order, General Hospital and Hawaii Five-O.
But it was his role in The Sopranos which brought Pastore widespread recognition. He appeared in all six seasons of the critically acclaimed show, despite his character being killed off in the second series.
In 2000, Pastore and his fellow The Sopranos cast members won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

title: Russian ship defies sanctions to send military vehicles to Mali
summary: The ship carried armoured personnel carriers and trucks through the English Channel to Africa, satellite images show.
full_text:
Russian ship defies sanctions to send military vehicles to Mali
- Published
Russian and Malian troops fighting against a rebel offensive in northern Mali have been resupplied with a vast number of military vehicles that appear to have been delivered by a sanctioned cargo ship, BBC Verify has found.
A large column of armoured vehicles were seen arriving in the capital Bamako in verified footage broadcast by Malian state TV on 25 July. Reporters said the convoy had travelled from Lomé port in Togo.
A sanctioned Russian cargo ship, Mikhail Britnev, docked in Lomé on 9 July, according to ship tracking data reviewed by BBC Verify. Satellite images appear to show that the ship was carrying the kind of trucks, armoured personnel carriers and light infantry vehicles seen in Bamako, according to experts.
Ship tracking data shows that the Mikhail Britnev left Russia's Baltiysk port on 18 June and moved through the North Sea before entering the English Channel.
BBC Verify understands that the vessel was escorted through the Channel by a Russian Ropucha-class warship. The UK's Ministry of Defence declined to comment.
Experts say the deliveries signify that the Kremlin is doubling down on its support for Mali's ruling junta, which has been rocked by the success of a rebel offensive led by the Jihadist group Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and Tuareg separatists. The advance has seized large swathes of territory in the north.
The Kremlin has backed the Mali military government since French forces withdrew from the country in 2022, receiving cash payments and preferential access to mines and gold deposits in return. At first the Russian mercenary group Wagner was deployed, but its operations have since been taken over by Africa Corps, which falls under Russia's defence ministry.
While BBC Verify has previously confirmed footage showing the unit carrying out air strikes against the rebel forces, the Africa Corps has struggled to halt their advance across the north of the country.
But Charlie Werb, an analyst with Aldebaran Threat Consultants, said the new shipment could help Malian and Russian forces to build up enough strength to launch offensives into areas which have fallen to the rebels.
The Mikhail Britnev was sanctioned by the US in 2024. Tracking data shows it switched off its transponder after passing through the Channel two weeks ago, and only reappeared when preparing to dock in Togo.
It was carrying a variety of military vehicles - including general purpose trucks, BTR-style armoured personnel carriers and light-infantry vehicles - according to experts who analysed satellite photos taken before it left Baltiysk port.
According to Malian state TV, the vehicles were then transported across Togo and through Burkina Faso - which is also ruled by a military junta backed by Moscow. The government in Togo has been deepening ties with the Kremlin and signed a military cooperation agreement with Moscow late last year.
The vehicles could be used for a mix of logistics and planning manoeuvres, as well combat operations, analysts at the defence intelligence firm Janes said.
BBC Verify understands that Baltiysk port has been the staging point for several ships exporting military materials to West Africa.
The bulk carrier Sabetta was tracked after loading what appeared to be military vehicles at the port in February. It docked at Conakry in Guinea, a port long associated with weapons transfers from Russia to its regional allies in West Africa.
Another tanker, which did not appear on ship tracking data, was also seen loading military vehicles at Baltiysk on 6 June.
Mali's military junta has suffered several battlefield setbacks in recent weeks. Rebel fighters have carried out sustained attacks on the northern town of Anefis, with clashes also reported near Niono and other parts of central Mali.
Amnesty International on Wednesday called for a war crimes investigation into what it said were the summary executions of at least 19 Malian soldiers after an ambush earlier this month.
But Werb said the delivery showed that the Kremlin was digging in to defend its allied junta.
"The Kremlin has maintained steady military support since the conflict entered a new phase on 25 April by bringing in fresh forces, weapons, and equipment," he said.
"The delivery highlights that despite recent setbacks, Mali remains central to Russia's strategy in Africa, and the Africa Corps is a key pillar in Bamako's fight against militant groups."

title: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
summary: After the Peak District signed a brand deal with Skoda, could other national parks follow suit?
full_text:
Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
- Published
A deal between Peak District bosses and car firm Skoda to put up temporary signs welcoming tourists to "the Peaq District" in honour of the firm's new electric model has given the park authority's coffers a welcome boost.
However, it has also sparked protests from campaigners and residents unhappy about the commercial aspect of the arrangement.
One campaigner said: "If national parks are prepared to sell their very name to the highest bidder, then we're already on the path to industrial extraction of the most protected landscapes."
Park bosses have defended the "fantastic" deal and said the partnership brought in extra funds for conservation and heritage work.
With national parks continuing to grapple with funding pressures, could the partnership be a sign of things to come for the Peak District and beyond?
Announcing the link-up, Skoda UK said the partnership was meant to "spark positive conversations" and to "encourage more people to get out and enjoy the Peak District in a responsible way". But campaigners are not convinced.
They told the BBC the partnership had raised "broader questions" about how national parks were funded and whether "increasing financial pressures" were leading authorities to seek commercial partnerships that "conflict with their environmental purpose".
National parks are primarily funded through the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), with the Peak District receiving £6m for 2025-26.
According to the Campaign for National Parks, external, government funding for National Park Authorities was reduced by 9% in that financial year, which it said had contributed to an estimated 40% real-terms reduction in funding since 2010 at a time when visitor numbers "continue to reach record levels".
The government says it is investing £37m in national parks over the next three years plus a further £30m for special habitats and species.
Phil Mulligan, chief executive of the Peak District National Park Authority, said the temporary rebranding was "exciting" and the money would help conservation, heritage and access works.
He declined to reveal the sum received but described it as a "reasonable amount".
Campaigner Harry Brook was part of a protest at one of the signs at Surprise View car park near Hathersage.
"I don't think what we have seen recently in the Peak District National Park is anyone's vision for the future of our national parks," he told the BBC.
"If you've had a sugar high, you're likely to go back again, aren't you?"
Brook added he "wholeheartedly sympathised" with Mulligan and said there was a lack of funding going into national parks.
However, he said: "It's silly we are at the point where we are having to resort to this type of funding to back national parks.
"Phil's said it himself, we're in a climate and biodiversity crisis, we know investing in our national parks is a strategic investment, so why are we having to resort to on the 75th anniversary of the park to selling the rights to the name?
"These landscapes are not there for commodification."
Asked whether he anticipated the negative response from some residents, Mulligan said he did because people were "passionate about the national park".
"The national park brings wonderful benefits to the nation and how it's here for everyone and how it's free for everyone," he said.
"But unfortunately, it's not free to deliver and with a declining government grant, we always seek to work in partnership with others.
"This Skoda promotion, I think, is fantastic... we're not actually changing the name of the national park, it's a one-week promotion.
"It allows us to receive a financial contribution that we can put to conservation, heritage, access works, so it's really positive.
"While I understand some people will have some concerns about it, it's quite standard really to have a very temporary digital takeover and I think it's for the enhancement and betterment of the national park and visitors."
Visitors approached by the BBC at Surprise View were both for and against the deal.
Dawn Fleetham disagreed with the rebranded sign.
"I don't think they should be doing that to the Peak District - somehow it just doesn't fit," she said.
A male visitor said: "I'm against some of the capitalist, advertisment stuff - it's like the same with football stadiums being named after brands. Having the traditional names is better in my opinion.
"I know they're giving [the park] money so it's good but it's a hard one."
Another visitor disagreed, sating: "It's just one sign... I think it's good advertising. It gets seen a lot."
But James Dawson said: "I thought it was a bit peculiar, the Peak isn't spelt that way, it's not spelt with a Q.
"I don't know what relevance Skodas have with the Peak District."
This is not the first time a corporate brand has partnered with a national park.
In the face of growing funding pressures, National Park Partnerships, external was established in 2016 specifically to create commercial relationships with places like the Peak District.
The partnerships fund conservation, visitor access, climate and community projects while allowing brands to associate themselves with protected landscapes.
One recent example is BMW UK, which formed a three-year "Recharge In Nature" partnership with national parks in 2022.
The aim was to to enhance the electric vehicle (EV) charging network across all 15 parks in the UK, while supporting a range of projects including nature restoration, biodiversity, regenerative tourism, and wellbeing initiatives.
Other brands involved with partnerships on conservation projects include high street bank Santander UK, mobile phone networks Vodafone and Three, and beauty giant Estée Lauder.
National Parks England executive director, Debbie Stockwell, said authorities needed to be "innovative" to raise money from a "range of sources".
"We welcomed the funding settlement from central government for 2026-2027, which enables national park authorities to deliver core services and projects," she said.
"However, over the last decade, the national park authorities that maintain these cherished places have faced the challenges of reduced central funding and rising costs.
"We are committed to diversifying our funding, and National Parks Partnership has been established to secure corporate and philanthropic giving.
"National Parks need to be innovative to raise income from a range of sources and were recently given increased powers by government in order to do this."

title: Emotional Kerr delivers moment Glasgow 2026 has waited for
summary: There were no pacers and no wave lights. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight.
full_text:
Saturday scrap ends with emotional Kerr winning fight
- Published
There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight.
Not his childhood pal and Scotland team-mate Jake Wightman. Not the Australian prodigy Cam Myers. Not the former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot.
This Commonwealth Games men's mile was his race, in his country, in front of his people. This gold medal really meant something.
Kerr's explosion of joy after he crossed the line and swaddled himself in a Saltire - having conducted the crowd during his final few strides - made that clear.
And so did his halting attempts to sing along with Flower of Scotland, the 28-year-old repeatedly stopping to bite his lip before wiping away tears from each eye.
"We rush through these moments so quickly," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland, having spent the best part of 45 minutes doing selfies and signatures. "So I was just telling myself to slow down.
"In my head, I was flashing through all the hard moments and realising that I've come a long way. And to have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different. Not many times in my career I'll ever have that."
- Kerr on why Commonwealth mile glory matters to him 
  - Published21 July
- Britain's Kerr breaks 27-year mile world record in London 
  - Published18 July
'I've had some pretty bad ones out there'
When Kerr crossed the line, the clock showed he was almost eight seconds slower than when running the fastest time ever for the mile in London last month. Three minutes 54.12 seconds.
What it didn't show was that for three of the four laps, this was more rammy than race.
Emerging between fireworks, Kerr had strutted out on to the track, spinning a bottle, and allowed his 12 rivals to sprint away. Only once they checked and began to run back did he stretch his own legs and acknowledge the crowd. Aura.
The 28-year-old also made sure to position himself between Myers and Cheruiyot on the start line. A flex, perhaps, but why not? Kerr has the credentials, after all. Former world champion, Olympic silver and bronze, the big dog in this fight.
And he needed all of his snarl and bite to survive the three laps of jostling, barging and bumping that followed.
The race was slow, too slow. And physical, really physical. Could Kerr - trapped in the pack, pinned to the kerb - deal with that? "As long as you stay on your feet, it's fine," was his assessment afterwards.
At the time, Kerr gave his answer as the bell tolled. In a flash, he made his move, bursting to the outside in pursuit of Myers and Cheruiyot, who made theirs momentarily first.
With 250m to go, Kerr left them behind. Wightman gamely tried to follow but how do you chase down a man this fast? His brave gamble failed and the bronze medallist from the last two Games trailed home in sixth.
By then, Kerr was already celebrating gold, with Myers coming through for silver and Cheruiyot bronze.
"I peeked up at the screen, saw I had a bit of a gap, and I felt great," added the Edinburgh athlete, who has been racing at Scotstoun since he was a child.
"I was just trying to stay present and enjoy it. I learned how to race on that track - and I've had some pretty bad ones out there - so to really enjoy that last 100m was a really important moment."
It was the moment Glasgow 2026 has been building to. The historic, reinstated, Blue Riband event of these Games got a fittingly elite winner. As a student of the sport's history, Kerr will appreciate that.
And as a kid who was at the athletics event at Hampden in 2014, he knew how much joy every man, women and child inside this place would derive from every picture he had taken, every word he shared with them, and every scrawl of his name.
"I have to take my time out there because they've waited and put their hard-earned money to come out and watch me perform," he said.
"You've got to stay in your lane and realise I'm lucky coming into this championship healthy, ready to go and I'm in the best shape of my life. And to do that in front of a home crowd is very special."

title: Shittu 'robbed' - are AI boxing judges the answer?
summary: After commentators claim England's Dimeji Shittu was "robbed" in the Commonwealth Games final, is judging helped by artificial intelligence the answer?
full_text:
Shittu 'robbed' - are AI boxing judges the answer?
- Published
The pundits made their feelings known.
"Shocking. Terrible. Totally robbed," said former champion Richie Woodhall.
England's Dimeji Shittu had to settle for silver at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday after a controversial defeat by India's Ankush Panghal.
Shittu, 24, was docked a point in both the second and third rounds but even without that, he would not have won after more controversial decision-making.
"The referee has cost Shittu the contest," Woodhall said on TNT Sports. "He has been robbed. I really feel for him."
It meant one of boxing's oldest talking points - how it is officiated - reared its head again. Would judging run or supported by artificial intelligence help solve this problem?
What happened to Shittu?
Shittu was well-placed in his final after winning the round on all five of the judges' scorecards. One punch resulted in Ankush receiving a standing count.
The contest swung in the second round, however.
Despite Shittu appearing to land the majority of the blows, three of the judges gave the round to Ankush.
It meant when a point was harshly deducted for dipping his head low, the Englishman was trailing overall.
Then when Shittu was punished for the same offence again despite hurting Ankush through the final round, the contest was effectively decided.
"Do me a favour, referee," said Woodhall as the second penalty was given.
"That is dreadful, absolutely dreadful," said TNT commentator Dave Farrar.
Remarkably, four of the judges still gave the final round to Ankush which meant the point deductions did not even matter. Shittu would have lost without them.
"How did [Ankush] win that last round on the scores 4-1?" Woodhall said.
"Absolutely terrible. Shocking. That is not sour grapes."
What did Shittu say?
Shittu, to his credit, refused to get drawn into the debate afterwards.
He appeared distraught as the result was confirmed but said "whatever the referee says goes".
"A lot of people might say this about the referee, the judging, but at the end of the day I can only blame myself," he told BBC Sport.
"Those are the rules. We live and we learn.
"At the end of the day, it's a foul in amateur boxing. It cost me the fight.
"If people think I should have got the decision, fair play, I understand.
"But if I'm sitting here blaming judges, blaming refs, I'm not going to get better."
What about AI?
Delicious Orie, England's superheavyweight champion from the 2022 Commonwealth Games, was another who believed the result was unfair.
"The referee has stripped the medal from Dimeji," he told TNT Sports.
And Orie went on to suggest introducing AI into boxing judging would be a way to improve the situation.
The topic has been discussed increasingly in recent years with the technology being used to judge Tyson Fury's bout with Oleksandr Usyk, external behind the scenes in 2024.
Under president and former unified world champion Gennadiy Golovkin, World Boxing, which runs amateur boxing around the world including at the Olympics and Commonwealth Games, has made moves to look into the implementation.
Nothing is imminent but the desire is there to investigate whether AI it could help improve transparency and integrity.
Traditionalists, though, may feel that subjectivity is simply part of the sport.
Technology has been used in other sports but more often for factual situation – was a forward offside, did a forehand land out, was there an edge of a cricket bat?
Would AI be able to determine the power of a punch? Are all punches equal? Those are issues that need to be considered.
"I wouldn't necessarily be against it," Orie said.
"Then it becomes an objective sport. If I knew there was a specific set of scoring then yeah, bring AI.
"I would follow that rule book rather than someone's opinion."
