〈西門町小羊卡牌「養套殺」捲3億跑路！1.5萬人一夜被刪群，實體店信任神話幻滅〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
臺北西門町知名寶可夢卡牌店「小羊卡牌社」今（3）日凌晨無預警刪除所有LINE群與社群帳號，實體店面大門深鎖，鄭姓負責人疑已於7月30日出境潛逃。超過1.5萬名玩家一覺醒來發現群組全消失，連夜成立自救會，粗估受害金額高達3億元，萬華分局已受理報案。
（前情提要：一張寶可夢卡賣 5.17 億元！日本政府要監管了）
（背景補充：AAX Line群解散！傳假員工私訊詐財、臺灣使用者墜樓）
西門町成都路上一家專營日版寶可夢（PTCG）卡牌的店面，今年初才風光開幕，今（3）日凌晨3時許，3個各5000人的LINE社群同時遭刪除，IG、Facebook同步關閉，實體店面鐵門深鎖——「小羊卡牌社」在一夜之間從卡牌圈徹底消失，留下逾萬名受害玩家與粗估高達3億元的未兌現訂單。
一夜之間人間蒸發
據瞭解，小羊卡牌社今年1月在西門町成都路開設實體店面，主要經營日版寶可夢卡牌代購、卡牌寄賣以及代送美國PSA、日本等第三方鑑定服務。憑藉實體店面與活躍的LINE社群經營，迅速在臺灣卡牌收藏圈累積知名度，旗下擁有3個5000人上限的官方LINE群組。
然而，8月3日凌晨3時許，這3個LINE群突然變成「無法使用的聊天室」，IG與Facebook也同步關版。受害玩家在社群平台Threads湧現大量災情文，連夜另闢群組成立自救會，人數從凌晨的數百人迅速擴張至3800人以上。有網友指出，早在7月30日就有人拍到鄭姓負責人在桃園機場出境的畫面。
受害內容涵蓋預購未出貨的寶可夢卡牌、寄賣在店內等待出售的高價收藏、以及已送交等待海外鑑定的卡片。個人損失金額從剛入坑玩家的7200元，到VIP會員高達數十萬元不等。一名玩家在Threads上無奈表示：「第一次到實體店買就被騙，以為有店面就很安全，結果半夜跑路。」
「養套殺」手法與卡牌市場熱潮
值得注意的是，多位玩家與業內人士指出，小羊卡牌社在事發前數週突然祭出一連串「讓利」促銷——包括烈空座、寶可夢30週年等熱門商品的預購優惠，吸引大量玩家下單付款。這種先以低價讓利累積信任、再一舉收割的手法，與加密貨幣世界常見的「拉地毯騙局」（rug pull）或「養套殺」模式如出一轍。
近年來集換式卡牌（TCG）已從單純的收藏興趣，演變為另類投資標的。動區曾報導，一張稀有寶可夢卡牌可賣到5.17億元天價，迫使日本政府成立跨黨派卡牌議員聯盟，研擬監管偽卡、囤貨與洗錢問題。卡牌市場的高單價與流動性，讓玩家願意將價值數十萬甚至上百萬元的收藏交由店家保管——然而寄賣、代購、代送鑑定等模式本質上屬於「信任託付」，一旦店家惡意倒閉，玩家的實體資產便面臨全額損失的風險。
官方回應與消保機制
臺北市法務局主任消保官林傳健今上午派員至小羊卡牌社公司登記地址稽查，現場大門深鎖無人應答。他說明，截至上午10時40分，臺北市政府尚未接獲正式消費申訴，但若業者無預警停業，已構成債務不履行，消費者有權請求返還已支付價金並賠償損害。法務局已橫向通報警方刑事警察大隊，釐清是否涉及詐欺罪嫌。
萬華分局證實已受理多起報案，將依法通知鄭姓負責人到案說明，詳細受害金額與人數仍待進一步統計。
一名自稱小羊卡牌社前員工的網友也在社群發文表示，自己僅負責客服與社群經營，未接觸金流，同樣在今天才發現聯絡不上負責人，7月份薪資至今未領，「本人也是此次事件的受影響者之一」。
實體店不再等於安全？數位時代的信任反思
「以為有實體店面就很安全」——這句話在Threads上被受害玩家反覆提起，也精準點出此事件的核心矛盾。在加密貨幣領域，中心化交易所倒閉（如FTX）、託管平台失能的教訓，讓「not your keys, not your coins」成為基本共識；而在實體卡牌收藏圈，將高價資產寄放在店家手中，本質上也是同樣的「託管信任」問題。
隨著集換式卡牌逐漸成為資產配置的一環，如何建立可信賴的第三方保管、鑑價與交易機制，正從愛好者圈內的閒聊話題，升格為監管與消費者保護的嚴肅課題。消保官呼籲受害玩家保留購買證明、付款紀錄、對話截圖與預購單據等4類證據，以利後續求償。

title: Arthur Hayes：聯準會本週 H.4.1 報告揭密日本日債抵押通道
summary:
BitMEX 共同創辦人 Arthur Hayes 提醒，本週聯準會 H.4.1 報告將揭密日本是否以國債為抵 […]

〈Arthur Hayes：聯準會本週 H.4.1 報告揭密日本日債抵押通道〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
BitMEX 共同創辦人 Arthur Hayes 提醒，本週聯準會 H.4.1 報告將揭密日本是否以國債為抵押幹預匯率。
（前情提要：美財長貝森特待辦清單走漏「百億日圓買單」！日圓匯率短線急升）
（背景補充：摩根大通：美財部幹預日元火力有限，理論上最多可動用 1,870 億美元）
比特MEX 共同創辦人 Arthur Hayes 8 月 3 日在 X 上指出，投資人應該關注本週即將公布的聯準會 H.4.1 報告，藉此確認日本財務省是否正透過國債抵押來創造美元，以幹預日圓匯率。
「如果美國財長成功提高對手方限額，聯準會就能以日本財務省的國債作為抵押品來創造貨幣。」他在 X 上表示。
https://x.com/CryptoHayes/status/2084099323772690719
H.4.1 報告是什麼？
H.4.1 是聯準會每週發布的資金統計報告，記錄銀行體系中的儲備金、聯邦基金利率和抵押品狀況。透過這份報告，Hayes 指出可以追蹤日本財務省是否先將國債賣出換取美元，再以這些美元購買日圓來支撐匯率。
日圓幹預鏈條
Hayes 提到的操作路徑如下：
- 日本財務省將持有的國債進行回購換取美元
- 用美元購買日圓，推升日圓匯率
- 美國財長貝森特提高對手方限額，讓聯準會能以日本國債作為抵押品創造貨幣
這套操作本質上是「以國債為抵押的貨幣創造通道」。一旦啟動，聯準會的資產負債表規模可能隨之擴張。
同日訊號：5 年期日債殖利率創 2000 年新高
就在 Hayes 發文同一天，日本 5 年期國債殖利率上行 5 個基點至 2.075%，創下 2000 年上市以來的新高。這顯示日本債券市場正處於價格重估階段，也間接印證了 Hayes 所說的操作路徑正在發生。
摩根大通同日分析指出，美國財部幹預日元的火力有限，理論上最多可動用 1,870 億美元，但這對於維持日圓匯率來說可能仍具影響。
Hayes 本人也在加碼
值得注意的是，Hayes 本人也在同一天進行了加密貨幣增持動作。據 Onchain Lens 監測，Hayes 在過去 1 小時內購買了約 250 萬美元的 ETH，另有 250 萬美元的交易待處理。他分別向 Galaxy Digital 和 FalconX 傳送 250 萬 USDC，從 Galaxy Digital 收到 1,337 枚 ETH。
Hayes 同時看多加密貨幣市場並關注日圓匯率戰，顯示他認為日圓貶值壓力下，資金可能持續流向美債→美元→加密貨幣的流動性通道。

title: BIT 報告：比特幣期權偏度放大，但下行風險訊號正在修復
summary:
BIT Official 每日圖表指出，比特幣期權偏度雖短期擴大，但已構築更高的低點，暗示市場對下行風險的極端 […]

〈BIT 報告：比特幣期權偏度放大，但下行風險訊號正在修復〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
BIT Official 每日圖表指出，比特幣期權偏度雖短期擴大，但已構築更高的低點，暗示市場對下行風險的極端擔憂正在消退。
（前情提要：比特幣選擇權「看跌情緒消散」！Glassnode：Put/Call 比率急降，防禦部位大解除）
（背景補充：Matrixport：比特幣市場情緒「極端樂觀」，小心短期回撥！）
BIT Official 8 月 3 日發布每日圖表分析，指出比特幣期權偏度的負值雖然再次擴大，但該指標可能正在構築「更高的低點」（higher low），暗示市場對下行風險的極端擔憂逐漸消退。
分析強調，這一判斷的前提是比特幣能夠守住 62,000 美元 的支撐區域。目前市場整體部位仍相對輕量，預期潛在拋售壓力有限。
📊#BIT今日分析 | 比特币期权显示下行风险正在缓解
比特币期权偏度的负值再次扩大，但我们认为，该指标可能正在构筑一个更高的低点（higher low），表明市场对下行风险的极端担忧或已逐渐消退。
这一判断的前提是比特币能够守住 62,000… pic.twitter.com/9eXGeEykZP
— BIT官方华语 (@BITofficial_CN) August 3, 2026
期權偏度訊號：更高的低點
期權偏度（skew）是衡量市場對下行風險恐懼程度的指標。負值越大，代表交易者對跌勢的防禦性買入越積極。BIT Official 指出，儘管偏度負值短期擴大，但從趨勢來看，每一次低點的幅度都在上升。
這意味著：市場不需要像上一輪那樣恐慌 就能建立防禦部位。若本週期權偏度負值確實收窄，比特幣有望恢復上漲走勢。
近期同步訊號：短期持有者虧損拋售創新高
同一日，CryptoQuant 分析師 Darkfost 指出，比特幣短期持有者在前一日以虧損將超過 32,000 枚 BTC 轉出至交易所，創下近一個月最大規模的虧損拋售。同期間，BTC 價格也短暫跌破 63,000 美元，現報約 62,999 美元，24 小時跌幅 0.8%。
不過，BIT Official 認為這些短期波動尚未形成連鎖反應 — 整體部位不重，賣壓空間相對可控。
宏觀逆風：地緣與美債收益率雙重壓力
分析同時提醒，本週仍需關注兩項宏觀風險：
- 地緣政治局勢：中東與東歐局勢持續推升避險情緒
- 美國國債收益率上升：10 年美債殖利率近期走高，壓縮風險資產估值
若這兩股力量在本週同步加劇，期權市場的修復訊號可能延遲顯現。

title: 輝達宣告共同封裝光學 CPO 進入量產，光通訊打強心針
summary:
輝達資深副總裁 Gilad Shainer 宣告共同封裝光學（CPO）已進入量產階段，與臺積電合作開發的 CP […]

〈輝達宣告共同封裝光學 CPO 進入量產，光通訊打強心針〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
輝達資深副總裁 Gilad Shainer 宣告共同封裝光學（CPO）已進入量產階段，與臺積電合作開發的 CPO 交換器開始交貨，預計 2026 年下半年全球 AI 工廠將迎來首批大規模匯入。
（前情提要：黃仁勳GTC 2026重新定義 PC：Vera Rubin 成首款 Agentic CPU）
（背景補充：黃仁勳：NVIDIA 要蓋「太空算力中心」！Vera Rubin Space-1 計畫）
輝達（NVIDIA）資深副總裁 Gilad Shainer 在近日舉行的技術論壇上宣告，共同封裝光學（CPO）已正式步入量產階段。輝達與供應鏈合作開發的交換器（Switch）目前已交付給緊密合作的客戶，同時也在輝達自家設施內部署。業界預期，今年下半年將開始看到大量具備 CPO 技術的交換器在全球各地 AI 工廠中匯入。
CPO 量產不只是宣告，輝達已完成供應鏈布局
Gilad Shainer 指出，輝達在任何技術量產前，都會提前打造好相關供應鏈。從光引擎（Optical Engine，OE）、封裝、光纖陣列（Fiber Array）到客製化雷射光源，輝達都有投資。他同時表示，輝達樂見產業技術標準化，後續亦會共同參與相關規定製定。
據瞭解，Shainer 主要負責輝達 InfiniBand 及乙太網路高速傳輸技術研發。他先前在網路傳輸架構大廠 Mellanox 負責研發，自 Mellanox 被輝達收購後，就加入輝達主持 AI 平台網路傳輸通訊相關部門，並與臺積電共同開發 COUPE 矽光子封裝平台。
Scale-up 是 CPO 最大商機，頻寬需求達 Scale-out 十倍以上
Shainer 特別強調，未來光通訊市場最大的成長引擎落在垂直擴充（Scale-up）領域。他指出，Scale-up 所需頻寬效能將會是水平擴充（Scale-out）的十倍以上，這代表 CPO 技術將先在高密度運算架構中發揮最大效益。
目前 CPO 已匯入在 Spectrum-X 平台，目標是配合新一代 Vera Rubin 即將到來的大規模部署。Vera Rubin 平台運算速度相較 GB300 提升至少三倍以上，對應的網路交換器頻寬自然也必須同步升級。
市場規模 2030 年上看 390 億美元，2028 年後才是放量關鍵
根據研調機構集邦科技（TrendForce）預估，CPO 與 NPO（Near-Optical-Processing）市場規模將於 2030 年突破 390 億美元。2028 至 2029 年間，成長動能將隨 Scale-up 開始匯入光互連後急遽增長。
不過值得注意的是，Shainer 這番發言也間接回應了幾個月前 SemiAnalysis 的看空報告，當時指出 CPO 良率不佳、量產可能延宕到 2028 年。如今輝達高層親自證實 CPO 量產進度按時推進，為光通訊市場帶來樂觀情緒。
臺灣語境：光通訊是臺灣供應鏈的隱形優勢
CPO 量產對臺灣產業鏈意味著什麼？臺灣在光模組、光通訊零元件領域已有深厚的製造基礎，從光引擎到雷射光源，臺灣供應商都佔據重要位置。輝達與臺積電合作開發 COUPE 平台，更直接將臺灣的先進封裝技術納入 CPO 供應鏈的核心環節。
雖然 CPO 放量出貨可能要等到 2028 年，但現在就卡位供應鏈的廠商，無疑將是下一波 AI 基礎設施投資的最大受惠者。對臺灣而言，這不僅是光通訊產業的契機，更是 AI 運算基礎設施從「晶片」延伸到「互連」的戰略轉移。

title: 高盛上調三星電子目標價至49萬韓元，AI記憶體供不應求至少延續到2028年
summary:
高盛最新研報將三星電子12個月目標價從48萬韓元上調至49萬韓元，預期AI記憶體需求將持續超越供給到2028年 […]

〈高盛上調三星電子目標價至49萬韓元，AI記憶體供不應求至少延續到2028年〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
高盛最新研報將三星電子12個月目標價從48萬韓元上調至49萬韓元，預期AI記憶體需求將持續超越供給到2028年。
（前情提要：高盛看爆：儲存缺貨飆到2028，三星海力士集體上調）
（背景補充：三星強漲記憶體 20%！瑞銀上修報價：DRAM Q3 季增 32%、NAND 漲 30%）
高盛在8月3日發表最新研報，將三星電子（005930.KS）的12個月目標價由48萬韓元上調至49萬韓元。該行指出，三星第二季營業利潤符合預期，並上調2026至2028年每股盈利預測約2%。
記憶體需求飆升，供不應求至少延續到2028
高盛在研報中強調，全球記憶體需求正大幅超越供給。該行預估2027年供需差距將進一步擴大，即使到了2028年，供給仍將維持偏緊狀態。
這項判斷延續了高盛今年6月的看法。當時高盛指出，AI訓練對高效記憶體的強烈需求正在重塑記憶體產業格局，DRAM 與 NAND 的產能擴張速度都跟不上資料中心的需求增長。
長期協議鎖定利潤，下行風險有限
高盛特別提到，三星已與主要資料中心客戶簽訂長期供應協議。這些合約不僅提供較佳的盈利能見度，也為三星在價格波動期間提供了下行保護。
在記憶體價格走勢方面，瑞銀7月初的報告指出，DRAM在第三季將季增32%、NAND漲30%，三星本年初已調漲DRAM價格約20%。
HBM4 提前佔據主力地位
三星正積極瞄準成為AI記憶體市場的領導者。高盛預期，新一代HBM4產品將在2026年下半年佔據三星HBM收入的逾60%，顯示三星在高頻寬記憶體領域的技術布局正在快速轉化為實際營收。
HBM（高頻寬記憶體）是AI晶片不可或缺的配套元件，NVIDIA H100、H200、H100 GPU 以及 AMD MI300 系列都依賴HBM提供資料傳輸。三星與SK海力士目前主導全球HBM供應鏈。
估值偏低，股東回報空間上看50%

title: Coldcard 災情延燒！遭竊比特幣增至 8,860 萬美元，受影響錢包恐全被掏空
summary:
硬體錢包 Coldcard 漏洞事件持續延燒。研究機構 Galaxy Research 最新指出，駭客仍持續盜取受漏洞影響的錢包資產，目前已確認遭竊比特幣增至約 1,367 枚，價值約 8,860 萬美元。研究團隊警告，只要使用受影響裝置建立的單簽錢包仍存有資產，最終都可能遭掏空，呼籲用戶立即轉移資產。

〈Coldcard 災情延燒！遭竊比特幣增至 8,860 萬美元，受影響錢包恐全被掏空〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
硬體錢包 Coldcard 漏洞事件持續延燒。研究機構 Galaxy Research 最新指出，駭客仍持續盜取受漏洞影響的錢包資產，目前已確認遭竊比特幣增至約 1,367 枚，價值約 8,860 萬美元。研究團隊警告，只要使用受影響裝置建立的單簽錢包仍存有資產，最終都可能遭掏空，呼籲用戶立即轉移資產。
根據 Galaxy Research 發布的調查，研究人員已偵測到駭客發動的「第三波」攻擊，這次再有 207.73 枚比特幣遭捲走，使目前確認失竊比特幣增至約 1,367 枚，按現價計算約 8,860 萬美元。
研究團隊表示，目前已確認有 4,585 個錢包地址受到影響，且攻擊仍在持續進行。
研究機構：攻擊尚未結束，受影響錢包恐遭全部清空
Galaxy Research 指出，這起事件並非一次性的資產盜竊，而是持續進行中的攻擊行動。
研究團隊警告，只要資產仍存放在由 Coldcard 受漏洞影響韌體版本生成的單簽錢包內，都有遭駭客轉走的風險，建議用戶立即將資產轉移至新的安全地址。
Galaxy Research 同時透露，已整理出約 600 個疑似駭客使用的鏈上地址，並通報美國聯邦執法機關、合規審查公司及資安專家，希望協助追蹤遭竊資金流向。
研究團隊也表示，許多受害者主動提供交易紀錄，協助研究人員分析鏈上資金流向與攻擊模式，讓調查得以持續推進。
Galaxy Research 持續追蹤受害地址，呼籲立即轉移資產
Galaxy Research 研究主管 Alex Thorn 在社群平台 X 發文表示，目前仍持續更新受害者與攻擊者地址資料庫。他強調：
我們仍在持續調查，並將新的受害者與攻擊者地址加入資料庫。這起攻擊尚未結束，如果你的資產仍存放在 Coldcard 生成的地址，請立即轉移。
隨著遭竊金額持續攀升，Coldcard 漏洞事件已成為近年比特幣自託管領域最受矚目的安全事故，也再次凸顯硬體錢包本身仍可能因韌體或金鑰生成機制漏洞而面臨重大安全風險。
根據《區塊客》先前報導，這個漏洞可追溯至 2021 年 3 月 Coinkite 推出的 Coldcard 韌體更新。由於當時程式設計出現錯誤，裝置在建立助記詞時使用的隨機數不足，使攻擊者得以透過演算法推測私鑰，進而控制錢包資產。
Alex Thorn 認為，從目前攻擊模式來看，駭客的掃描與竊取流程高度自動化且具規律性，不排除是利用大型語言模型協助分析與篩選受害錢包。
他警告，只要是 2021 年韌體更新後建立的單簽 Coldcard 地址，未來都有可能遭駭客洗劫，只是時間早晚的問題。
Galaxy 指出，這些遭竊比特幣在被盜前，平均已有 3.18 年未曾移動，顯示受害者多為長期持有者。截至目前，這三波攻擊所竊取的資金仍停留在駭客控制地址，尚未進一步轉移或出售。
這起事件也讓不少用戶陷入恐慌。多位資安專家提醒，用戶在轉移資產時仍須提高警覺，避免將資金轉入同樣存在風險的新地址。
值得注意的是，許多受影響用戶正加速將比特幣從自託管錢包撤出，轉而存入 Coinbase 、幣安等中心化交易所，或重新建立新的安全錢包地址。

title: 獲利跳水、 AI 「搶電搶錢」！比特幣「挖礦難度」自今年高點重挫 14%
summary:
比特幣網路迎來史上罕見的「算力退潮」。受幣價走弱、挖礦收益縮水，以及資金與電力資源轉向人工智慧（ AI ）運算需求影響，比特幣挖礦難度已自今年高點回落約 14%，更是史上第二次跌破前一年同期水準，反映全球挖礦算力明顯衰退。

〈獲利跳水、 AI 「搶電搶錢」！比特幣「挖礦難度」自今年高點重挫 14%〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
比特幣網路迎來史上罕見的「算力退潮」。受幣價走弱、挖礦收益縮水，以及資金與電力資源轉向人工智慧（AI）運算需求影響，比特幣挖礦難度已自今年高點回落約 14%，更是史上第二次跌破前一年同期水準，反映全球挖礦算力明顯衰退。
算力競爭壓力暫緩
鏈上數據顯示，在經歷微幅下調 0.74% 後，比特幣目前的挖礦難度來到 126.23 T，較去年同期的 127.62 T 下滑 1.1%，若與 2025 年 11 月創下的歷史高點 155.97 T 相比，跌幅深達 19.1% 。
比特幣區塊鏈每挖出 2,016 個區塊（大約兩周）就會依據算力的高低變化進行難度調整，以確保無論有多少礦工在挖礦都仍然能夠維持「每 10 分鐘產出一個區塊」的速度。
挖礦難度基本上反映了礦工之間的競爭水平，難度越高則競爭越激烈。如果在過去兩周，算力上升，那麼挖礦難度也會跟著上升，讓比特幣挖礦更難。如果算力下滑，那麼挖礦難度水準也會降低，使礦工更容易解開區塊。
數據顯示，繼 6 月、 7 月初分別下修 10% 及 5% 後，比特幣挖礦難度已較今年 1 月的高點大幅衰退約 14% 。
值得注意的是，這是比特幣史上第二次出現挖礦難度低於前一年同期的現象。
第一次發生在 2021 年中國全面禁止比特幣挖礦後，當時約有半數全球算力瞬間下線，導致挖礦難度大幅下降。不過隨著礦工陸續遷往美國、哈薩克等地，網路算力很快恢復成長。
然而，這一次造成挖礦難度下降的原因，並非政策打擊，而是整體挖礦經濟惡化。
利潤遭壓縮，礦企棄守「比特幣」擁抱「AI」
礦業數據平台 Luxor 旗下的 Hashrate Index 分析指出，比特幣價格疲軟與挖礦收益遭到嚴重壓縮，迫使礦企不得不將資金、電力資源以及營運重心，大舉轉移至 AI 與高效能運算（HPC）基礎設施。
此外，美國德州夏季用電限制（Curtailment）以及其他主要挖礦地區供電中斷，也進一步削弱整體算力。
收益指標探底，礦業凜冬未完待續
遺憾的是，難度下調並未替礦工帶來太多喘息空間。
用來衡量礦工單位算力預期收益的「哈希價格（Hashprice）」，在 6 月下旬一度慘跌至每日每 PH/s 27.66 美元，距離今年 2 月的歷史低點僅有一美分之遙。儘管近期雖已回升至約 31.7 美元，但仍遠低於過去牛市水準，營運壓力依然沉重。
展望後市，根據 Luxor 遠期市場的定價數據，預估至今年 12 月底，哈希價格的平均水準約落在每日每 PH/s 31.85 美元左右，僅略高於目前水平。
這代表市場普遍預期，2026 年剩餘時間內，比特幣礦工的獲利能力恐怕難以出現明顯改善。在挖礦收益持續受壓、 AI 基礎設施快速擴張的背景下，全球比特幣挖礦產業仍將面臨新一輪轉型與洗牌。

title: 比特幣 7 月逆勢收漲 7%！分析師：強制平倉賣壓已耗盡、 8 月恐維持震盪
summary:
即使面臨聯準會（Fed）升息預期升溫、美債殖利率攀高、AI 概念股重挫，以及 Coldcard 冷錢包漏洞事件等多重利空，比特幣仍展現出優於美股的抗跌能力。分析師指出，市場歷經大規模去槓桿化之後，強制平倉賣壓基本已消化殆盡，短期內真正影響行情的因素，不外乎總體經濟數據與加密貨幣 ETF 資金流向。

〈比特幣 7 月逆勢收漲 7%！分析師：強制平倉賣壓已耗盡、 8 月恐維持震盪〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
即使面臨聯準會（Fed）升息預期升溫、美債殖利率攀高、 AI 概念股重挫，以及 Coldcard 冷錢包漏洞事件等多重利空，比特幣仍展現出優於美股的抗跌能力。分析師指出，市場歷經大規模去槓桿化之後，強制平倉賣壓基本已消化殆盡，短期內真正影響行情的因素，不外乎總體經濟數據與加密貨幣 ETF 資金流向。
根據 CoinGlass 數據顯示，比特幣 7 月以上漲約 7.36% 作收，在近期市場接連遭遇多重利空衝擊下，這樣的表現仍優於不少投資人的預期。
過去幾周，市場陸續消化 Fed 可能在今年再度升息、美債殖利率攀升、 AI 類股大幅回檔，以及知名硬體錢包 Coldcard 爆發安全漏洞等事件。然而，比特幣並未出現市場原先擔憂的深度修正，而是在熊市低點之上持續整理，即使其他風險資產承壓，也展現出相對韌性。
比特幣抗跌優於美股，去槓桿成關鍵原因
Bitfinex 分析師指出，比特幣之所以比股票市場更具抗跌性，主要來自市場部位結構已提前完成調整。
分析師表示，在 Fed 利率決議公布前，加密貨幣市場的槓桿水平已明顯低於股市。原因是在 6 月底至 7 月初、比特幣跌破 58,000 美元期間，衍生品市場已歷經一波大規模強制平倉，大量高槓桿部位提前被清洗出場。
自那之後，Bitfinex 觀察到，市場每日平均清算金額一直低於今年常見的 4 至 5 億美元水準，顯示即使近期總經利空接連出現，也未引發新一輪大規模強制性拋售潮。
分析師表示：「相較於高槓桿的 AI 等股票題材，加密貨幣市場跌幅較小，原因就在於強制賣壓早已提前釋放。」
Coldcard 漏洞引發安全疑慮，自託管風險再受關注
除了總體經濟因素外，市場近期也持續消化 Coldcard 硬體錢包安全漏洞事件的影響。
Galaxy Research 統計，Coldcard 上周至今共爆發 3 波攻擊，累計有 1,367 枚比特幣（約 8,900 萬美元）遭竊，再次引發市場對自託管安全性的討論。
交易公司 Wincent 董事 Paul Howard 表示，目前遭竊資產尚未出售，因此尚未直接衝擊市場價格，但若駭客未來開始變現，短期內仍可能對比特幣造成一定賣壓。
他指出，這起事件再次提醒市場，自託管雖然是加密貨幣的重要理念，但同時也伴隨著不可忽視的操作與安全風險。
市場聚焦非農就業與 ETF 資金流，8 月恐陷區間震盪
展望後市，分析師普遍認為，市場焦點仍將回到總體經濟。 STS Digital 管理合夥人 Jeff Anderson 表示，目前市場正進入新的波動階段，投資人持續在降息、暫停升息與再次升息等不同預期間反覆修正，使高波動資產持續承受壓力。
他認為，在經濟前景更加明朗之前，包括比特幣在內的高 Beta 資產仍可能維持震盪。
Bitfinex 分析師則表示，下周即將公布的美國非農就業報告（NFP），將是繼 Fed 利率決策之後，最重要的總體經濟觀察指標，預料投資人將維持防禦性姿態。
分析師認為，比起擔憂下一波斷頭潮，目前市場真正關心的是：當 Fed 的貨幣政策路徑更加清晰後，比特幣現貨 ETF 的資金能否大舉回流？Bitfinex 表示：
只要升息風險尚未完全解除，市場部位將持續偏向防禦。真正值得交易員關注的訊號，是機構投資人是否展現出積極、甚至「不在乎價格（Price-agnostic）」的強勁買盤。
Bitget Wallet 研究分析師 Lacie Zhang 則預估，8 月基準情境仍將是區間震盪。她表示，除非實質殖利率下降，或比特幣現貨 ETF 資金流重新持續轉正，否則比特幣短期難以突破盤整格局。她指出：
市場可以消化聯準會維持利率不變，但若美元持續走強、實質殖利率上升，加上 ETF 資金需求疲弱，三項因素同時出現，將對比特幣形成更大的壓力。

title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
summary: Theo became the first British baby to be operated on in the womb to correct complex gastroschisis, as part of a pioneering clinical trial.
full_text:
Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
- Published
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.
His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.
Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.
Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.
He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.
Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.
"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.
But they both know things could have been very different.
The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.
For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.
Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.
Theo's parents initially had no idea anything was wrong with their unborn child.
"Going towards a 20-week scan, we were purely just excited to have an image of our baby," said Josh. "We didn't know he was going to be a 'he' at the time."
Josh said discovering Theo had gastroschisis had been a shock and "incredibly scary".
At 24 weeks gestation, specialist doctors at London's Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) had been preparing expectant parents Maisie and Josh for what the first six months of Theo's life were going to look like.
However, after discovering he had the more serious condition of complex gastroschisis, doctors referred him to Texas Children's Hospital, in Houston.
There, a team of foetal and paediatric surgeons, led by Dr Michael Belfort, had been leading a first-of-its-kind clinical trial to repair complex gastroschisis before birth.
Belfort, the clinical lead on the trial, had previously pioneered a similar surgical procedure in the womb on babies with spina bifida.
Maisie was told she would have to travel to Texas straight away and remain there for the rest of her pregnancy. "It was a huge decision," she said.
As part of the trial she first had to travel to Leuven Hospital, in Belgium, where specialists needed to give Maisie a Botox injection through her womb into Theo's abdominal wall, to relax the muscles to make the repair easier.
The family then flew to Texas where the operation was performed in November last year, 26 weeks into the pregnancy.
Josh said he had had an agonising wait while doctors had operated on Maisie. "The length of that day, it felt like a week," he said. "The waiting and just not knowing exactly what was going on at each and every stage."
Maisie's womb was partially exposed to position the uterus and baby, the amniotic fluid was drained and replaced with carbon dioxide (CO2) gas to expand the operating space. Using keyhole surgery, Theo's organs were then gently pushed back inside his abdomen, which was stitched closed.
Maisie was left with a scar, twice the size of a C-section incision. But unlike other women who are recovering from a C-section, she still had a baby to grow inside her for another 14 weeks.
She said Theo would often kick inside her, hitting her scar and causing her pain. "It was a hard recovery," Maise said. "But, it was worth it."
The operation was a complete success and Theo was carried to term and born in February by vaginal delivery in Texas.
Belfort, obstetrician and gynaecologist-in-chief at Texas Children's Hospital, said he and his team are very happy with the results so far.
"The mother, the baby, the surgery, the time of the surgery, the fact that we had zero complications during the foetal surgery and after the foetal surgery, just remarkable."
If the trial is a success, Paolo de Coppi, professor of paediatric surgery at GOSH and head of stem cells and regenerative medicine at University College London, would perform the procedure in the UK.
"We hope that we will be able to offer this to patients in a larger scale very soon," he said.
Belfort is excited about the partnership and said Texas Children's and GOSH working together will be a formidable team.
And Belfort is already looking ahead to what he can do next.
"The inside of the uterus is now a new surgical space for innovation," he said. "And spina bifida and gastroschisis are just two, but I believe that we could actually do certain cardiac surgeries in utero, and I think we can also do some lung surgeries in utero."
Back home in London, Maisie said Theo is doing amazingly.
"Everything they did just completely reversed what could have been a really horrible start to his life and he's just the best. He's a completely normal baby essentially."
"We both feel incredibly fortunate," Josh said. "The impact that they've had on us as a family is incredible. They made us feel so welcome from the team at Great Ormond Street to Dr Belfort and the team.
"Whilst we were over there, the level of care was amazing, and they made a very traumatic time of our lives so much easier, and we've got this little man - we couldn't be happier."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

title: Wales first nation to withdraw support for Infantino
summary: Wales become the first nation to publicly withdraw backing for Gianni Infantino's bid to continue his leadership of Fifa.
full_text:
Wales first nation to withdraw support for Infantino
- Published
Wales have become the first nation to publicly withdraw backing for Gianni Infantino's bid to continue his leadership of Fifa.
It follows the loss of confidence in the Fifa president following his scrapped plans to sell stakes in its competitions to private investment firms.
The Football Association of Wales (FAW) has confirmed "its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term".
Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.
Uefa and Concacaf - which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - both released statements on Saturday criticising the leadership of the world governing body following Infantino's decision to withdraw the plan.
The FAW added: "The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football.
"Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept."

title: Inside city gripped by deadly protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
summary: The BBC gains unique access to Rawalakot, scene of violent clashes between security forces and protesters in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
full_text:
'My only son was shot standing up for justice' - inside city gripped by deadly protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
- Published
Dr Anwar's makeshift clinic is not far from the main protest site in the city of Rawalakot in Pakistan-administered Kashmir (PAK). A spare bedroom acts as a medical supply cupboard, outside is a bed under a red stretched tarpaulin.
Lying across the bed is Shafqat Hussain, shot in the chest. The sheet he lies on is already stained with the blood of previously injured. He is dying.
In the last two months, dozens of people have been killed across the region in clashes between security officials and protesters from the group Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).
This region - home to about 4.5 million people - currently has elections taking place.
The BBC is the first media organisation to gain access to Rawalakot and speak to those at the heart of the protests.
Dr Anwar – whose name, like most of those in this report, has been changed to protect contributors – tells our team: "We have enough supplies to provide first aid. We can stop bleeding, clean and dress wounds, and remove superficial bullets. But patients with serious injuries to the chest, abdomen, head, or other vital organs need advanced hospitals."
Anwar adds: "Even major hospitals would struggle if many such patients arrived at the same time."
Since 27 July, the clinic has treated around 50 to 60 critically injured patients, the doctor says, adding that he personally treated 15 to 20 with gunshot wounds.
Protesters are scared to go to the main hospital because they fear they will be arrested or shot. The authorities have said that claim is inaccurate.
"Most of those who have been killed or seriously injured are young people between about 15-16 years old and 32-35 years old. I have seen very few patients over the age of 40."
At Hussain's bedside is his friend Ali. He wipes his tears away with his shawl.
"We only asked for affordable flour, electricity and our basic rights," he says, trying to steady his breath through his sobs. "Instead, our brothers are being killed. What was our crime? Why are live bullets being fired at us?"
Protesters from the JAAC say the demonstrations are about their rights, with concerns including electricity prices, education and health care. An agreement signed with the Pakistan and PAK governments back in October was meant to help. The JAAC says it's not been implemented.
The local government disagrees. They say the group is armed and that this is about disrupting the ongoing polls. And they are not willing to let the protesters march to the regional capital, Muzaffarabad.
The JAAC was banned in June; they have been labelled foreign-funded terrorists. They reject this characterisation, saying they are peaceful and - though funded from the PAK community abroad - not sponsored by India.
Rather than initiating violence, they say they are the victims and that Pakistan's security forces have been firing on them.
With the internet cut and roads blocked or guarded, getting information has been difficult.
Once in the city, the BBC spoke to multiple families who say they lost loved ones, shot at the protests.
Asma said she was at the protest herself when she heard her only son had been shot.
"We were only asking for our rights. We are not terrorists," she said. "No mother could ask for a better son."
"He knew there were risks, but he believed standing up for justice was important. He used to say that dying for a just cause was an honour."
Salman lost his brother.
"He was the youngest in the family and was loved by everyone. It is a great loss for us," he said.
"At the same time I feel proud that he gave his life while standing up for the rights of the people. He was not fighting or attacking anyone."
Ayub was formerly in the armed forces and lost his son. He did not blame the Pakistan government or military, but instead pointed to the government in PAK, saying they were the ones who called in the paramilitary forces.
"I am a retired soldier. I lived through the martial law periods of General Zia-ul-Haq and General Pervez Musharraf," he said. "But I have never seen anything like what is happening now. In my opinion, it is extreme injustice."
"My son had done nothing wrong. None of the protesters had done anything wrong.
The government for PAK has said that it rejects the allegations the security forces fired indiscriminately upon peaceful protesters, saying that law enforcement acted against individuals who were involved in attacks on law enforcement personnel, threatened public safety or obstructed lawful authority.
The BBC witnessed food shortages, with many protesters sharing what they had with one another. Most shops were shuttered. Some told the BBC of efforts to smuggle in bags of rice on the backs of motorbikes.
Some roads into the city have been blocked by felled trees; the authorities say this was done by the JAAC. Other entry points on the main road now have security checkpoints. PAK's government said that it was false to suggest that they were preventing food or medical supplies from entering Rawalakot, saying instead that they were facilitating its entry.
The authorities have repeatedly said that the JAAC are a violent group and have shared drone shots of what they say are JAAC members carrying guns on rooftops.
At news conferences, police officials have displayed guns they say they have taken from the group, telling local media of the injuries and deaths of security officials. They said that under interrogation one man said he had been promised a reward of 10 million rupees (around £26,700) for every paramilitary officer killed.
This was denied by Umar Nazir, a member of the JAAC's core committee and currently in Rawalakot. But security officials have lost their lives.
"Look, perhaps such deaths did occur - I will not comment on that," he said.
"However, I believe that certain elements, who are under their control, were infiltrated into our ranks. Such people were certainly present among us."
"I believe they may have carried out such actions themselves in order to justify their own narrative. I am not making a definitive claim, but there is no evidence whatsoever that any such violence came from our side."
He provided no evidence to support this claim of an alleged infiltration and the authorities have said that the JAAC have engaged in a campaign of disinformation against them, particularly on social media.
At the JAAC protests we attended, the BBC saw no sign of weaponry or shooting, although overnight repeated gunshots were heard. It was unclear who was shooting or at what.
The atmosphere was tense and uncertain; no-one knows when the situation could escalate.
Nazir says that the group are willing to talk, but for now, more protests are planned.

title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
summary: Discipline at an academy trust went too far - parents, pupils and former teachers tell BBC Panorama.
full_text:
How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
- Published
To avoid getting into trouble at school, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water so she would not need the toilet.
Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.
New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.
Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.
Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena run its schools - and their vocal opposition now appears to have paid off. Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.
It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".
BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.
The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.
"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.
Athena is not the only academy trust that has enforced strict discipline.
There are those who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils - and exam results at Athena-run schools have improved.
About 20% of the school day in England is lost to bad behaviour, the government says.
The benefits of a "high level of strictness" is that students understand what is expected of them, says the government advisor on behaviour in schools in England, Tom Bennett.
Commenting generally, rather than on individual academies, he told us that pupils soon realise they have to get into the habit of meeting expectations.
However, there is growing concern that punitive disciplinary practices at some schools in England are damaging children.
Britain’s Strictest Schools
How much discipline is too much? Panorama investigates the academy trust where classrooms are silent and pupils can be sent to detention for looking out of the window.
Watch on iPlayer now or on Monday 3 August at 20:00 on BBC One.
Athena's secondary schools are attended by about 6,500 children. In the past three years, more than 500 children have left to be educated at home, according to Cornwall and Devon county councils.
Amelia is one of them.
While at Camborne, Amelia would often come home with the bottle of water she had left with in the morning still full.
When Kayley asked Amelia why, she says her daughter would reply that she had not drunk anything all day, "so I wouldn't need to go to the toilet".
Camborne has strict rules around toilet visits during lessons.
Pupils were not allowed to go to the toilet in the first or last 15 minutes of a lesson, and were only allowed to go in the middle of a lesson at the teacher's discretion, pupils and former teachers told us.
Kayley believes her daughter's fear of breaking the rules ended up making her ill.
"She's now on antibiotics, she's had water infections, she has got scarring on her kidneys because of this," Kayley says.
Amelia says her time at Camborne "makes me feel ill, even thinking of it".
Athena told Panorama that staff work hard to "support children to remain in education" and "support access to toilets during lessons" through professional staff judgement.
Academies are independent, state-funded schools, that receive their funding directly from central government, rather than through a local authority. They have independent control over their own admissions, curriculum and staff pay.
There are no academy trusts in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but more than 80% of secondary schools in England are now run by them.
Multi-academy trusts like Athena oversee a network of schools. Athena's reports from the regulator, Ofsted, have mostly been positive.
Brian Maywood used to be the head of Launceston College in north Cornwall and was an English teacher there when Athena took over.
Initially he welcomed the trust's highly disciplined approach, and was pleased the school was "moving into a new way of learning".
But his opinion quickly shifted, he says, once he witnessed how the children were treated, calling it a "dictatorship".
The way students were spoken to at times "made me really, really uncomfortable", he adds.
He left the school last summer because of these reasons, he says.
It was the same for the former head of art, Estelle Pears.
"There is discipline and then there is being oppressed," she says. "It sounds dramatic, but that's what it became.
"If you're frightened of moving a pencil on a desk because you will get a sanction, that's beyond discipline."
Former Athena teachers who spoke to Panorama said they were forced to uphold the strict rules by the trust and that some made little sense.
Ieuan Horgan says his music lessons had to be taught in silence.
"At the start of the lesson, I would go through how to play the musical notation, and then the lesson would just be silent focus on trying to learn this musical notation," he says.
"They pushed for 100% distraction and disruption-free lessons - and 100% silent focus - in a music lesson."
Pupils have told Panorama they could be punished for minor offences and Bethany, who has just finished her GCSEs at Camborne, describes the strict and regimented approach as "demoralising" and "like you're being talked to like you were a primary school kid".
Athena schools have a two-strike policy: a warning for one mistake, sent out of the class for the second. Students then go to what is called "reflection" - a room where they work in silence from workbooks.
At Launceston College there were about 1,000 cases a month of pupils being sent to "reflection" rooms between September 2025 and March 2026, according to figures released by the trust.
Athena says reflection rooms are "supervised environments" where "students continue their learning independently".
It says it does not have a rigid two strikes policy and the "vast majority of students spend little or no time in these spaces". Students are not normally punished for isolated minor issues, it adds.
Some parents say children with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by Athena's strict policies.
April, whose son Jack has special educational needs and has just finished his GCSEs at Ilfracombe Academy, says he was sent to reflection countless times.
He could not cope with the regimented environment, she says.
"Just to look out the window to refocus, that's not harming any of the other children or their education within the room - but that's enough to be sent out, because that's him not focusing on the teacher."
Jack was also suspended - sent home from school - dozens of times. He is far from alone.
The suspension rate at Ilfracombe Academy was almost five times higher than the average in England, according to government figures for 2023 to 2025. At Camborne, it was about five times higher than the average and three times higher at Launceston, according to the same figures.
Athena says suspensions are reserved for "serious or repeated breaches of behaviour expectations" and that rates have fallen significantly in the past year.
April and Jack's concerns were echoed at our town-hall events. More than half of the dozens of parents and pupils who turned up were concerned about the impact on students with special educational needs.

title: Glasgow praised for saving Commonwealth Games as baton passes to Amdavad
summary: The head of Glasgow 2026 believes the legacy of the scaled-back Games will shape the future of the event.
full_text:
Glasgow hailed for saving Games as baton passes to Amdavad
- Published
The man responsible for delivering Glasgow 2026 said the city had "saved and reinvented" the Commonwealth Games, three years after its future was plunged into doubt.
Ahead of Sunday's closing ceremony - which featured a dazzling fireworks display over the River Clyde - Phil Batty recalled how Glasgow stepped up when the original hosts pulled out.
And he believes the legacy of the sustainable, scaled-back Games will shape the future of the multi-sports event.
The Commonwealth flag was last night ceremonially handed over to the Indian city of Amdavad, which will stage the centenary event in 2030.
But Batty said Glasgow's decision to host the event for a second time in 12 years would never be forgotten.
He told BBC Scotland News: "We have created a Games here that will inspire more nations to host but, probably more importantly, that every nation feels it could host at some point in the next 100 years."
Simple Minds brought the curtain down on an 11-day sporting festival during the closing ceremony at the Hydro on Sunday.
As athletes from 74 nations and territories looked on they opened with Alive and Kicking.
It was appropriate song choice for an event that was, not too long ago, on life support.
In July 2023 the Australian state of Victoria withdrew from staging the Games due to soaring costs.
But in September 2024 Glasgow, with support from the Scottish government, agreed to a put on a scaled-back event.
Batty said the city had, over the last 11 days, answered any questions around the relevance and, indeed the existence, of the Games.
He told BBC Scotland News: "I don't think we can underestimate that the future of the Commonwealth Games was in jeopardy.
"Glasgow saved the Commonwealth Games but it also reinvented the Commonwealth Games."
He said this process included re-formatting sports for the future.
"It isn't about saving something to preserve it. It is about reinventing something to give it the purpose and vision it needs to last," he added.
Batty said the event was for far too long "hosted by the few and not the many".
But he added: "This is a really important moment for the movement to become a truly Commonwealth-wide global sporting competition.
"Glasgow and Scotland should be incredibly proud, of not what only has happened here but what that means for the whole Commonwealth in the years and decades to come."
The Glasgow 2026 boss described how the Games may develop.
He explained: "It may be a twin nation host in Asia, it may be a multi-island host in the Pacific Islands, It might be an absolutely compact multi-venue model in Africa.
"This will look different in every edition but, importantly, it will now be designed to the place that is hosting."
Batty said the privately-funded event had been delivered over 18 months on "triple speed" compared to a typical build-up of six years.
Its projected cost is £162.6m compared to £543m for Glasgow 2014 and £680m for Birmingham 2022.
Batty said it was "fuelled by the legacy" of the last Games in the city and more environmentally stable.
This follows as it used existing venues and infrastructure within an eight-mile radius.
The more compact 23rd edition featured 215 medal events compared to 261 when the city last staged the Games in 2014.
It also saw a record 47 para-sports events, which included the symbolic first gold medal.
It was won by English lightweight powerlifter Mark Swan.
The following day organisers were dealt a major blow when reigning 10,000m champion Eilish McColgan pulled out with a foot fracture.
But new heroes stepped up for the host nation, most notably swimmer Angharad Evans who won two golds, a silver and a bronze.
Further inspiration was found in the pool by in the shape of Archie Goodburn, who is fighting brain cancer.
Scotland's Melanie Woods won gold in the 1500m T54 for the second time in under 40 hours after the final was restaged.
Her victory, in a new record time, was recognised at the closing ceremony when she was named the outstanding athlete of the Games.
And para cycling great Neil Fachie bowed out with the seventh gold of his career.
Australia dominated the medal table by amassing 171 followed by England with 110.
The host nation finished fifth, with 39 medals, behind Canada and India, a performance described by First Minister John Swinney as "truly historic".
Records also tumbled in the velodrome, on synthetic carpet and in the pool, as fans were treated to some world-class sporting action.
Welsh star Emma Finucane created history by becoming the first sprint cyclist to win four track gold medals at the same Games.
Louise Hoskins became the oldest Commonwealth Games gold medallist, winning the para-bowls women's pairs title for Australia at the age of 76 years and 173 days.
And legendary South African swimmer Chad le Clos became the most decorated athlete in the 96-year history of the event with 21 medals.
Empty seats were visible at many events but organisers said they exceeded their targets by selling more than 430,000 tickets.
The action unfolded across four venues - each powered by renewable energy - with the most noticeable buzz around the SEC Campus.
Netball at the Hydro proved to be box office by selling 100,000 tickets.
Batty said the Games had been able to grow the fan base and make it the single largest attended sport in the programme.
On Saturday Prince William and Princess Kate were among those who took in the action with their children.
Elsewhere, Tollcross International Swimming Centre was a cauldron of noise during the medal events.
And Scotstoun Stadium was the scene for everything from a biblical downpour on Tuesday to a race for the ages on Saturday night.
Indeed those who witnessed world record holder Josh Kerr's thrilling triumph in the mile - which last featured at the Games in 1966 - will never forget it.
The star repaid fans for their support by taking 45 minutes to pose for selfies and autographs after his emotional medal ceremony.
Glasgow's famous sense of humour was a common thread throughout the Games.
The sight of the King and Queen emerging from a Tardis at the start of the opening ceremony in the Hydro stunned the audience.
And Callum Beattie's performance of the Scotland football anthem Yes Sir, I Can Boogie - featuring silver unicorns and dancing Barrowland-style stars - put a smile on everyone's face.
At the end a giant Tunnock's Teacake rocket took off on stage, in tribute to the dancing versions from the 2014 opening ceremony at Celtic Park.
It later appeared to have landed at the Games Live site in Kelvingrove Park, where it provided a popular photo opportunity.
More than 200,000 visited the west end park and live sites in the city during the Games.
Fun was also injected some fun into proceedings at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in the east end.
Before every race the cycling legend appeared on the big screen and bellowed: "Hoi you lot! Shhhh."
Swimmer Duncan Scott, who won his fourth Commonwealth gold, then added: "Haud your wheesht" - a traditional Scots phrase meaning "be quiet."
On Sunday, Team Scotland stood out at the closing ceremony with traffic cone hats, in a nod to the iconic Duke of Wellingston statue.
Away from the action the Games mascot Finnie proved a merchandising hit.
Small cuddly toys of the unicorn sold out in store and online before the weekend.
Meanwhile, athletes and Games staff continued the long standing tradition of collecting team pin badges, resulting in some impressive bling lanyards.
And throughout all the action an army of 4,000 volunteers - aged 16 to 96 - kept everything running smoothly.
During the closing ceremony George Black, chair of Glasgow 2026, described them as "the heartbeat of the Games".
Amdavad's staus as the 2030 hosts was recognised on Sunday with a colourful explosion of dance and performances by major Indian artists.
Before then, Malta will stage the Commonwealth Youth Games from 29 October to 4 November next year.

title: Aung San Suu Kyi appears healthy in first confirmed outside contact for 2.5 years
summary: Photos newly released by Myanmar's military government show Suu Kyi meeting with an ICRC official.
full_text:
Aung San Suu Kyi appears healthy in first confirmed outside contact for 2.5 years
- Published
The detained Burmese leader Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to meet a delegation from the International Federation of the Red Cross, the first confirmed outside contact with her for two and a half years.
In photographs of the meeting released by the military government Suu Kyi appeared to be healthy.
She was detained shortly after the armed forces deposed her government in 2021, and sentenced to 33 years in jail on what are widely viewed as trumped up charges, though her sentence has been reduced and she has been moved to house arrest.
Despite repeated assurances from the military authorities that Aung San Suu Kyi is alive and well, they have never provided any convincing evidence of this.
Her son Kim Aris has in recent months mounted an international campaign demanding proof of life for the 81-year-old democracy icon.
Now a delegation from the ICRC has been allowed to meet her – her first confirmed meeting with anyone outside the government for nearly four years.
Photographs released of her with the ICRC team show Suu Kyi looking relaxed and well, although no details of her state of health have been given, nor of what they talked about.
The Myanmar government, still headed by coup-leader Min Aung Hlaing and dominated by the military despite an election held earlier this year, is trying to end its diplomatic isolation in a series of official visits to neighbouring countries.
Among the top demands being made of Myanmar's military leadership is that they end the aerial bombardment of opposition-held areas, start negotiations to end the civil war, and release Aung San Suu Kyi.
They have so far rejected those calls, but the publication of this morning's meeting suggests they may be willing to accede to the last demand.

title: 'Nothing is strange' - how clubs prepare for the transfer window
summary: Premier League clubs have already spent more than £1bn in the transfer window, but are expected to only get busier.
full_text:
'Nothing is strange' - how clubs prepare for the transfer window
- Published
Premier League teams have already spent more than £1bn this transfer window.
Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham have all splashed out on players costing £100m or more, each a record-breaking deal.
Sandro Tonali's £100m move to Spurs was eclipsed by Elliot Anderson's £116m switch to Manchester City and that was followed by Chelsea setting a new record for a British player by signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117m.
The spending follows on from a winter window in which clubs spent 2.2bn euros worldwide.
But the financial muscle of the Premier League is unmatched. So, with billions at stake, how do clubs prepare to get moves over the line?
The modern ways clubs discuss deals
In February, about 100 club officials, scouts and agents gathered at Villa Park for a networking event.
Over coffee and pastries, in William McGregor's in the Trinity Road Stand, representatives from clubs including Liverpool, West Ham, Birmingham, Preston, Derby, Aston Villa and Manchester City chatted, along with agents, to prepare for the summer and debrief the winter.
In the afternoon, Villa's head of emerging talent and loans Adam Henshall gave a presentation on how the club oversees its loaning out of players - outlining the data, the risk and reward elements they take into consideration before sending their young talent out.
Henshall had been asked to provide insight into Villa's workings by TransferRoom, which uses its online platform to connect clubs and agents, potentially initiating or accelerating moves.
About 800 clubs have signed up and, this week, Villa, Chelsea, Crystal Palace, Manchester City and United, Roma and Borussia Dortmund will be among more than 200 who will meet with 55 agencies in Madrid for a 'deal day' where moves can be finalised. Online events are held too.
The aim is to aid clubs in a window which is expected to erupt in the second half of August, clubs having been unable to get the majority of deals done early because of the World Cup.
Meanwhile, clubs in the English Football League are finding they have to wait for those at the top to make their decisions to kick-start the market, even if plans are well in place.
Ideally, clubs aim to work at least one window ahead, with one senior Premier League recruitment executive insisting anything else is "reactionary".
In the top flight, clubs will know who is most likely to move and can plan in advance.
It is vastly different lower down where there is the acceptance that, if a player is performing well, they could be likely to move on.
Essentially, any player is tradeable, leaving sporting directors and managers to firefight.
Many lower EFL clubs also look to time moves to save on wages, signing someone later in the window meaning they might save weeks' worth of salary payments.
The amount of data used in recruitment also varies greatly throughout the leagues - platforms analysing players are available, but the cost of accessing means that some clubs in the lower leagues will not be able to justify the expense.
But for all, planning starts early with work on the summer window typically starting almost immediately after the winter window.
"It'll be a couple of weeks after the January window shuts," says former Portsmouth, Blackpool, Oxford and Shrewsbury boss Michael Appleton.
"The closer you get to the window opening, your meetings become a lot more regular.
"At the start of March, I'm sitting down with the recruitment team once a week but once you get closer to the window that becomes every few days and then leading into the window, possibly every day."
Much, though, will depend on the club's network. In some instances, they might contact an agency 12 months before a move, discussing the contract or estimated fee, but other moves will be just days from initial contact to completion. One lower league club has previously searched for targets' agents on Instagram.
All, though, will try to gather as much information as possible on their target list - even if they know they will not land them all.
Fire's Lewandowski move 10 years in the making
One of the biggest moves this summer, despite being a free transfer, saw Poland captain Robert Lewandowski join MLS side Chicago Fire after his Barcelona contract expired.
Fire had been eyeing Lewandowski for a decade, believing they could convince him to come to America, especially with the large Polish community in Chicago.
"That sounds ridiculous because at that stage he was in the prime of his career and scoring goals for Bayern and then Barcelona, but it shows the long-term planning," Fire sporting director Gregg Broughton tells BBC Sport.
It became a reality in January 2025 when Fire were in negotiations for Neymar, who shares the same agent - Pini Zahavi - as Lewandowski.
While Neymar opted to return to Brazil with Santos, it was made clear then there was a possibility to sign Poland's record scorer.
Being on Fire's 'discovery list' meant no other MLS club could sign the forward - but they still had to bide their time, waiting for Barcelona to make their decision on the 37-year-old's future and being unable to speak directly to Lewandowski until 1 January.
That call was made quickly afterwards and boss Gregg Berhalter flew to Spain to meet him.
"The rest of the club is building the structure around it with his representatives because when you've got a player of Robert's stature, it's not just a straightforward contract," says Broughton.
"There are commercial negotiations to be had. What did that look like in terms of his own future career beyond football? What did it mean for his wife?
"His wife has her own very successful fitness business. What did that look like opening up to an American market? Where are his children going to go to school? What kind of school do they go to in Barcelona?"
Lewandowski made his first trip to the city in June and was met with a fanfare of 'welcome to Chicago' billboard messages from the drive from the airport.
"I'm not sure you'd do that between Heathrow and Chelsea," joked Broughton.
"My concern as the sporting director was: 'how are we going to keep this under wraps?' I was looking purely through a European lens and the Americans are: 'we're not going to, because that's not how we treat free agents in American sport. We're going to go big on it.'
It worked and Lewandowski signed a two-year deal, as Fire held off European and Saudi interest.
"The signing is evidence the plan is working," added Broughton.
Deadline day dawns
Some feel the growing influence of agents has made the window more complicated because they want more control in club-to-club agreements. The amount of paperwork can also be increased adding to frustrations, even if there is a general acceptance that agents are a vital part of the system.
Agents will, understandably, want to see the paperwork and go through the AF1 document - the agency agreement which details the deal, which agents worked on it, how much they will be paid and how. Clubs can view it as another layer to a deal and a further complication.
Yet with deadline day just a month away, agents are only going to get busier - though there is a sentiment from some at the top of the Premier League that if sides are pulling together deals on deadline day they are likely to be a mistake.
Those in recruitment in the top flight feel that, ideally, clubs should have been in a position at least 72 hours before the deadline to make a move.
The majority of big deals are done weeks in advance and, if they go through in the final hours, it is usually just because numbers still had to be finalised.
"I like to get my work done before then, so you're not panicking and rushing about," adds Appleton. "But a lot of stuff on deadline day is more about preparing for players that you're going to lose or might lose and reacting quickly."

title: 'I did my first book signing in a police custody suite'
summary: The Northern Irish author has sold more than five million books globally and been translated into 40 languages
full_text:
'I did my first book signing in a police custody suite'
- Published
For former lawyer turned crime writer Steve Cavanagh, addressing a court room jury is not a world away from writing a compelling novel. Indeed the idea for his first book came to him while he was cross-examining a witness.
"I kind of conned them into revealing that they were lying and it hit me then that con artists and trial lawyers have all the same skills," he said.
The idea sparked something in Cavanagh, who has just released his tenth novel about the conman turned lawyer Eddie Flynn.
The Northern Irish author has now sold more than five million books globally and has appeared on the Sunday Times bestseller list.
Cavanagh's home, near Lisburn, is busy. His daughter pops in to say hello, Muffin the dog is looking for someone to throw a ball, he's not long back from a US tour promoting his last book and he's packing to leave the following day for a UK book tour.
It's something he never really thought would happen when he was working as a solicitor.
He grew up on Palestine Street in south Belfast, went to school in Ballynahinch, then onto Belfast tech before going to uni in Dublin.
He only started writing in his mid 30s, after his mum died.
Cavanagh said she was the only one who ever really encouraged him to write so he wrote his first book for her.
His surname is Mearns, but he used Cavanagh, his mother's maiden name as a tribute to her. It was also easier to separate the practising solicitor from the author.
Cavanagh sais that "every word is a weapon in a courtroom".
"I thought con artists and trial lawyers all have skills which are perfectly allowed: misdirection, distraction, persuasion, manipulation," he said.
"I thought that would be a good idea for a character, someone who had all those skills as a conman, who then becomes a lawyer and that's be an interesting character to write about."
That led to the birth of his character Eddie Flynn, a lawyer based in New York, aided by his associates Harry Ford, Melissa Bloch, Gabriel Lake and a dog named after Clarence Darrow, another inspiration of Cavanagh's.
It wasn't an easy start for Cavanagh, who was rejected by more than 50 agents before getting representation for the Eddie Flynn series and securing the first book deal.
He recalls publication day for his first book, The Defence. He was representing a client in a police station in County Down when one of the police officers said he'd heard he had released a book.
"I went in and did the interview and by the time I came out the old custody sergeant had been to Eason's and bought it, so I did my first signing in Bangor custody suite."
While the first book won awards, it didn't sell particularly well and it was only when Thirteen, the novel which Cavanagh describes as having changed his life, was released did things really take off.
He believes this was down to the books gripping tag line: "The serial killer isn't on trial, he's on the jury."
Readers took to it and in 2019 he was able to stop working as a solicitor to focus on writing.
He's written 10 Eddie Flynn books and a few stand-alone thrillers.
Author of The Housemaid, Freida McFadden, recently posted on Facebook about his thriller Kill for Me, Kill for You, saying it is "one of the best thrillers I've ever read".
"It's not often that I read a book where all the twists and turns are perfectly executed, but this is one of them. It's kind of a masterpiece, in my humble opinion," she said.
It's high praise from the hottest author around at the moment and Cavanagh is quick to return the compliment and also talk about other local authors who he thinks people should be reading.
Cavanagh has touched on a number of themes in his books. In Two Kinds of Stranger, he looks at a TikToker who has shared so much of her life online that she's become an easy target for a criminal mastermind.
In his latest book, One Of Us is Guilty, we meet the billionaire Vanderpool family and are immersed in a gruesome murder.
Patrick Vanderpool, who is running for governor, and his wife Vanessa are both in the firing line for the murder but Patrick's father Julian controls half of New York so will anyone really have to pay?
Cavanagh said he wanted to look at extreme power and wealth in America the influence of multi billionaires.
"I write about law and a lawyer, and increasingly these days, laws don't matter to some people," he said.
He is critical of AI companies.
"That entire technology is almost based entirely on piracy. They have scraped millions of books and the government's doing nothing.
"It's almost the more powerful you are, the more you can get away with."
For Cavanagh, this is a world away from his working class upbringing in Belfast.
He plans to take a break from Eddie Flynn for now, he has a standalone book in mind and has been asked by the Conan Doyle estate to write a short Sherlock Holmes story for a collection in the Autumn.
But he wants to reassure fans that Eddie Flynn will be back and hasn't been beaten yet.

title: 'Your legacy will live forever': Nepal mourns climber Nirmal Purja
summary: Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed some of the country's best mountaineers.
full_text:
'Your legacy will live forever': Nepal mourns climber Nirmal Purja
- Published
Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed all 10 members of an expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak, six of whom were Nepalese.
Among them was Nirmal Purja, also known as Nims, a British-Nepali climber most known for climbing the world's 14 tallest peaks in just over six months.
His death has sent shockwaves through the global mountaineering community and through Nepal, where he is a celebrated figure for giving a spotlight to Nepali climbing guides.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah was among those who paid tribute, saying his "history of courage, dedication and contribution will always remain inspiring".
In a moving tribute on Facebook, Purja's brother Kamal wrote: "I feel as though I have lost my whole world. My brother was not only my younger brother - he was my heart."
"Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added.
At the Small Heaven School in Chitwan district, near Kathmandu, which Purja had once attended, students and staff lit candles and mourned his death.
Sarbagya Paudel, one of the students at the vigil, said Purja's "bravery has set a great example for our school. Not only has he made our school proud, but he has also brought pride to Nepal".
Purja is still fondly remembered by those who had known him from his schooling days. Shailendra Baral, his school hostel supervisor, told AFP that as a young boy Purja had been "fearless and committed to achieving something".
"He was honest and an obedient student, which made us happy. We found courage in him even when he was a child."
Bahadur Panta, Purja's school friend, said he had prayed for the mountaineer through "sleepless nights" after news broke of his disappearance.
"It was not only me and my friends. I think people all over the world who knew him... prayed for him. But it was his fate, no one could avoid it," he told AFP.
Social media was also awash with tributes to Purja, with many saying that Nepal was in mourning and that the country had lost a "legend" and "many great climbers".
"Their legacy will live on," said one comment.
Purja was catapulted into international stardom after his journey was documented in a 2021 Netflix documentary.
Among his 10-member expedition on Broad Peak, there were six Nepali climbers. The other four climbers were from the US, China, Oman, Pakistan.
They had gone missing after being caught in an avalanche last Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak.
Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.
Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.
Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.
Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.
But as he became more famous, troubling allegations emerged about his conduct.
In 2024, a New York Times article detailed sexual allegations two women made against Purja. One alleged that he had sexually assaulted her in a hotel room in 2023 and another said he had grabbed and propositioned her while guiding her on an expedition to K2 in 2022. He denied these claims through his lawyer.
- Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Who is Nirmal Purja, the famed mountaineer killed in Broad Peak avalanche? 
  - Published18 hours ago
But while Purja may be the most recognisable face, he was not the only famed climber in the disaster-hit expedition on Broad Peak. The 10-member team also consisted of big names in Nepal's climbing community.
There was Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - who summitted Everest 10 times. In 2024, he was part of the team that discovered a century-old shoe on the world's tallest peak, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on Everest with George Mallory in 1924.
"Standing with you on the summit of Mount Everest is a memory I will cherish forever," fellow mountaineer and guide Uttam Lapraki wrote in a tribute to Yukta on social media.
"The Himalayas have lost one of their finest sons, but your courage, kindness, and legacy will continue to inspire generations of climbers."
Another member of the team, Kili Pemba Sherpa, was part of a historic 2021 expedition that summitted K2, the world's second-highest peak, in winter. That expedition was made up of all Nepali climbers, including Purja.
Imagine Nepal, an expedition company where Kili Pemba worked as a guide, wrote on Instagram that he had "stood with us from the very beginning, from the days we first started climbing together".
"He was humble in every way and never tired of helping climbers when they needed him. He was a foundation of our team and a part of every summit we have ever celebrated."

title: ‘Tell us’: Gaza family trapped between hope and pain over missing brothers
summary: The disappearance of two boys last year has turned the Abdel Aal family’s life into an endless search for answers.
full_text:
‘Tell us’: Gaza family trapped between hope and pain over missing brothers
The disappearance of two boys last year has turned the Abdel Aal family’s life into an endless search for answers.
Gaza City, the Gaza Strip – For more than a year, Ashjan Abdel Aal’s life has been suspended between grief and hope.
Two of her sons, Othman and Sami, have been missing since the morning of June 29, 2025, when they left their displaced family’s home in Gaza City – only never to return.
“I want them to come back,” the 36-year-old says through tears. “I want a day when I can see them, hug them and hear their voices.”
Ashjan remembers the last time she saw them.
The two brothers – Othman, who would now be 17, and Sami, 13 – said they would head to an aid distribution point near the so-called Netzarim Corridor in central Gaza, promising their six-year-old sister Emarat they would bring her sweets. Ashjan also recalls hearing that they might pass by the family’s old home in the Shujayea neighbourhood of eastern Gaza City – something they had also done previously – to bring back a pair of shoes for her.
The Abdel Aal family is one of the thousands to have been forced from their homes during Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip that has killed more than 73,340 people, according to health officials, and left much of the besieged and bombarded territory in ruins. Ashjan, her husband, Rafaat, and their children found shelter at a relative’s house in Gaza City in April last year, at a time when hunger, soaring prices and shortages of basic items pushed many people to take risks searching for food.
“People were either returning to dangerous areas or going to aid distribution points because they had no other choice,” says Rafaat, 41.
On August 1 last year, the United Nations said at least 1,373 Palestinians had been killed while seeking food since late May 2025 – 859 near aid distribution sites and 514 along the routes of food convoys.
On the day Othman and Sami left, Rafaat was away. He had also headed towards United States-backed aid distribution sites near the Zikim area in northern Gaza.
“I was there for a day and a half,” he recalls. “When I returned, my wife told me that the boys had not come back. I became very worried and started asking about them.”
The family waited through the evening, hoping, in vain, that they would return. On the following day, Rafaat began searching hospitals, displacement shelters and among relatives, but found no trace of his sons – since then, the boys’ disappearance has turned the family’s life into an endless search for answers.
Conflicting reports
The first potential lead came more than a month later. A resident of Shujayea told the family he had seen four bodies near their old home. Two had been identified, but the other two had not.
Rafaat says the descriptions he received resembled his sons, but the family could not confirm whether the bodies were Sami and Othman.
Then, two days later came another painful message. A relative shared a photo of an unidentified body at al-Ahli Arab Hospital, saying it looked like Othman.
“At first glance, I was deeply shocked,” recalls Rafaat. “I said this was my son Othman with 90 percent certainty. I went to the hospital, but when I saw the body, it was not my son.”
In October 2025, after Israel and the Palestinian group Hamas reached a “ceasefire” deal, Rafaat was able to reach the area near their old home in Shujayea. He found only destruction. “There was a piece of a missile, fragments and a small bone remnant,” he says.
But later, the family could no longer access the area since it fell behind the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control within Gaza.
The search continued through the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and human rights organisations, but no confirmed information was available.
At times, Rafaat says, the uncertainty became unbearable.
“During many moments, because of the immense psychological pressure, I thought about going to the civil registry and requesting official death certificates for them,” he says. “But even that was not possible because there were no witnesses or enough evidence confirming their deaths.”
Hopes and unanswered questions
Months later, in May, a new piece of information rekindled the family’s hopes. Rafaat received a phone call from his wife’s brother who had been helping him communicate with human rights groups, international institutions and lawyers.
“He called me and told me that a lawyer from inside the 1948 areas, who presented herself as someone following missing persons’ cases with human rights organisations and the Red Cross, had said that the boys were alive and in detention” in the Israeli prisons of Ofer and Naqab, says Rafaat.
Ashjan remembers that moment. “My husband told me, and we hugged each other and cried so hard,” she says. “We cried because we thought maybe they were coming back.”
The information, however, was never officially confirmed. The family tried contacting the lawyer again, but received no response. Al Jazeera also attempted to reach the lawyer, but the phone numbers provided by the family were not working.
“I am like a drowning person holding on to any straw,” says Ashjan. “My heart tells me they are alive. I see them in my dreams coming to me and telling me not to cry.”
She says before the boys’ disappearance, Othman, a teenager on the autism spectrum, would always notice when she was sad before anyone else. “He would try to comfort me in any way he could,” she says. “Because of his kindness, Sami became very attached to him. He followed him everywhere.”
Rafaat struggles to hold back tears as he listens to his wife describe their sons. He says the boys had tried to help the family despite his objections, going out in search of aid in the hope of bringing food home.
“Since they left, I feel like I am living in a cycle that never ends,” he says. “I cannot move forward, and I cannot stop thinking about what happened to them.”
Families trapped in uncertainty
The story of the Abdel Aal family reflects a wider struggle faced by many families in Gaza who are searching for missing relatives amid the absence of confirmed information and the spread of conflicting reports.
Gaza’s Government Media Office estimates that some 11,200 people remain missing across the territory, including those believed to be trapped under the rubble as well as others whose whereabouts remain unknown.
Nada Abu Aita, director of the Palestinian Centre for Missing and Forcibly Disappeared Persons, says one of the biggest challenges in documenting cases of missing people is what she describes as the “multiplicity of sources”.
She says the centre’s work depends on communicating with families, collecting details about disappearances and documenting the circumstances surrounding each case.
But for families already living through war, displacement and loss, not knowing the fate of a loved one creates another layer of suffering.
“They live in a state of uncertainty that prevents them from continuing their lives or even overcoming their grief for the missing person,” says Abu Aita. “In the morning, they search for hope that they will find them, and in the evening, they become certain that they have died.”
She says this painful uncertainty makes families more vulnerable to information from unofficial sources, especially when those sources offer the possibility of finding their missing relatives.
The lack of complete information from the Israeli side, even for international groups, leaves some families believing that unofficial mediators or lawyers may have access to information that established organisations do not.
Abu Aita says the centre has received many reports from families contacted by people claiming to be lawyers or representatives of organisations who told them that their relatives were being held in Israeli prisons.
But after examining some of these cases and checking the organisations these individuals claimed to repr

title: Grid failure plunges Cuba into nationwide blackout
summary: Cuba’s ageing power grid collapsed on Sunday after a weekend of outages and amid US-imposed fuel shortages.
full_text:
Grid failure plunges Cuba into nationwide blackout
Cuba’s electricity system has deteriorated amid shortages of fuel and replacement parts.
Cuba’s national electricity grid has collapsed, plunging the island into a widespread blackout.
The state-run Electric Union, known as UNE, announced the collapse on X late on Sunday but did not immediately identify its cause, the extent of the disruption or when electricity would be restored.
Before the nationwide failure, Havana’s electricity company had reported outages caused by damaged transformers, circuit failures, and planned cuts linked to insufficient generating capacity.
Recommended Stories
